passage.original:
عشق او باز اندر آوردم به بند
کوشش بسیار نامد سودمند
عشق دریایی کرانه ناپدید
کی توان کردن شنا ای هوشمند
عشق را خواهی که تا پایان بری
بس که بپسندید باید ناپسند
زشت باید دید وانگارید خوب
زهر باید خورد وانگارید قند
توسنی کردم ندانستم همی
کز کشیدن تنگتر گردد کمند
passage.english:
Once more his love has caught me in its bonds;
for all my struggling, nothing came of it.
Love is an ocean with no shore in sight:
how could anyone swim it, clever one?
If you would carry love on to its end,
you must accept much that you dislike:
see what is ugly and call it fair,
drink poison down and call it sugar.
I bucked and fought, and never understood
that pulling only draws the lasso tighter.

passage.original:
Në fytyrët tënde gjeta Bukurinë.
Si ajy që gjeti në malt Perëndinë
Lulezët e Majit sa janë të mira!
Po përpara teje m’erdhë të pështira.
Kur shoh faqezët’ e tua,
Ç’vjeft’ i mbetet trëndafilit,
Zëri yt shpirt më jep mua,
Nuk’ i le shije bilbilit.
Edhe yjt’ e hëna si të shëmëtuar
M’u duknë, kur pashë atë syn’e shkruar.
Purtek’ e florinjtë! shigjet’ e ergjëntë!
Zëmrënë m’a dogje, m’i përndave mëntë!
passage.english:
In your face I came upon Beauty,
as one who came upon God in the mountains.
How fine the little flowers of May are!
Yet next to you they seemed to me ill-favoured.
When I see your cheeks,
what worth is left to the rose?
Your voice gives me back my soul;
it leaves the nightingale no sweetness.
Even the stars and the moon looked dimmed to me
once I had seen that eye, as if drawn by a pen.
Golden rod! Silver arrow!
You set my heart on fire and scattered my wits!

passage.original:
وسلطان الجمال له اعتزاز
على ذي الخيل والرجل الجواد
وهذا الفعل مغتفر وزين
إذا يوماً أبيت على معاد
فإن رضيت علي أرت محيا
بشوشا بالملاحة ظل باد
خليلي إن أتيت إلي يوما
بشيراً بالوصال وبالوداد
فنفسي بالبشارة إن ترمها
فخذها بالطريف وبالتلاد
إذا ما الناس ترغب في كنوز
فبنت العم مكتنزي وزادي
passage.english:
The sultan of beauty carries itself proudly
above the horseman and the open-handed man;
and this is pardoned, and becomes it well,
if one day I may pass a night with a promise of meeting.
If she is pleased with me, she shows me a face
that smiles, its loveliness always plain to see.
My friend, if one day you come to me
with good news of union and of love,
and want my life as payment for the news,
take it, with all I have gained and all I inherited.
When people set their hearts on buried treasure,
my cousin is my treasure and my store.

passage.original:
Nesta pequena cidade,
vi uma certa donzela,
que muito tinha de bela,
de fada, huri e deidade,
a quem disse: - “minha q’rida,
peço um beijo por favor,
bem sabes ó meu amor,
que eu por ti daria a vida!”
- “Nguami-âmi, ngana-lame,
“não quero, caro senhor” –
disse, sem mudar de cor –
“maculo! quangandallâmi,
“não creio no vosso amor”...
passage.english:
In this small town
I saw a certain young woman,
blessed with great beauty,
like a fairy, a houri, a goddess,
and I said to her: “My dear one,
I ask you for a kiss, please;
you know very well, my love,
I would give my life for you!”
“Nguami-âmi, ngana-lame,
‘I don't want to, kind sir,’”
she said, without a blush;
“maculo! quangandallâmi,
‘I don't believe in your love’…”

passage.original:
Dos palabras tan dulces, que la luna que andaba
Filtrando entre las ramas
Se detuvo en mi boca. Tan dulces dos palabras
Que una hormiga pasea por mi cuello y no intento
Moverme para echarla.
Tan dulces dos palabras
Que digo sin quererlo — oh qué bella la vida —
Tan dulces y tan mansas
Que aceites olorosos sobre el cuerpo derraman.
Tan dulces y tan bellas
Que los dedos más largos de mi mano derecha
Se mueven hacia el cielo imitando tijeras.
Mis dos dedos quisieran
Cortar estrellas.
passage.english:
Two words so sweet that the moon, which was wandering,
sifting through the branches,
came to rest on my mouth. So sweet, two words,
that an ant is strolling along my neck and I make no effort
to move and send it away.
So sweet, two words,
that I say without meaning to — oh, how lovely life is —
so sweet and so tender
they pour scented oils over my body.
So sweet and so lovely
that the longest fingers of my right hand
reach for the sky, snipping like scissors.
My two fingers would like
to cut stars.

display.creator: Sayat-Nova

passage.original:
Քանի վուր ջան իմ,
Յա՜ր, քի ղուրբան իմ.
Աբա ի՛նչ անիմ.
Արտասունք անիմ,
Շատ հոքուց հանիմ,
Յա՛ր, ղադեդ տանիմ.
Ասիր՝ ջեյրան իմ.
Թուղ քի սեյր անիմ,
Յա՛ր, մըտիկ անիմ։
Մո՛ւտ բաղչեն նազով,
Քիզ գովիմ սազով,
Յա՜ր, իլթիմազով։
passage.english:
For as long as I live, my soul,
beloved, I am your sacrifice.
What else am I to do?
I will weep,
I will sigh from deep in my heart,
beloved, I will carry your sorrow.
I am your captive, my gazelle;
let me look at you to my heart's content,
beloved, let me gaze.
Come into the garden with your graceful air;
I will praise you on my saz,
beloved, with my entreaty.

passage.original:
But, Rose Lorraine—ah! Rose Lorraine,
I'll whisper now, where no one hears—
If you should chance to meet again
The man you kissed in soft, dead years,
Just say for once "He suffered much,"
And add to this "His fate was worst
Because of me, my voice, my touch."
There is no passion like the first!
If I that breathe your slow sweet name,
As one breathes low notes on a flute,
Have vext your peace with word of blame,
The phrase is dead—the lips are mute.

title: Liebes-Lied
creator: Rainer Maria Rilke
editionDate: 1907, Neue Gedichte (Leipzig: Insel-Verlag), p. 3
description: Two lovers are so bound together that the poet cannot keep his soul from touching hers: everything that moves them draws one voice from two strings, like a bow.
provenance: Rilke, Neue Gedichte (Leipzig: Insel-Verlag, 1907), p. 3; German Wikisource, transcribed from the 1907 scans.
translation: Work changed (30 October 2026): Ada Christen's “Erklärung”, a poem of distrust rather than love, is replaced by Rilke's best-known love poem. Complete poem, 13 lines. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI) made directly from the German, deliberately not following published translations; draft for editorial review.
rights: Anthology review (30 October 2026): published 1907; Rilke died 1926, so public domain in the UK, EU and US. Modern English translations (for example Stephen Mitchell's) are in copyright and are not used.
source: German Wikisource: Liebes-Lied (Neue Gedichte, 1907)
contextNote: Rainer Maria Rilke was born in Prague in 1875, when it belonged to the Austrian Empire, and became one of the great poets of the German language. “Liebes-Lied” appears near the start of his Neue Gedichte (New Poems, 1907), written in the years he spent in Paris learning from the sculptor Auguste Rodin to look closely at things.

passage.original:
Wie soll ich meine Seele halten, daß
sie nicht an deine rührt? Wie soll ich sie
hinheben über dich zu andern Dingen?
Ach gerne möcht ich sie bei irgendwas
Verlorenem im Dunkel unterbringen
an einer fremden stillen Stelle, die
nicht weiterschwingt wenn deine Tiefen schwingen.
Doch alles was uns anrührt, dich und mich,
nimmt uns zusammen wie ein Bogenstrich,
der aus zwei Saiten eine Stimme zieht.
Auf welches Instrument sind wir gespannt?
Und welcher Spieler hat uns in der Hand?
O süßes Lied.
passage.english:
How am I to hold my soul so that
it does not touch on yours? How am I to
lift it over you to other things?
Oh, I would gladly lodge it somewhere
with something lost in the dark,
in a strange, still place
that does not go on trembling when your depths tremble.
Yet all that stirs us, you and me,
gathers us up like a stroke of the bow
that pulls a single voice from two strings.
On what instrument are we strung?
And which player has us in hand?
O sweet song.

passage.original:
Şuri-eşqin başıma axırı sövda gətirir,
Bu müşəxəssdi ki, eşq aşiqə qovğa gətirir.
Tari-zülfündü məni böylə giriftar eləyib,
Nə gələ başıma, ol zülfi-mütərra gətirir.
Gül üzün görmək əgər mümkün olaydı bir dəm,
Hər zaman görmək onu nuri-mücəlla gətirir.
Qaşü göz, novki-mücə fitnə üçün cəm olmuş,
Ox atıb, tiğ cəkib, hər biri dəva gətirir.
passage.english:
The frenzy of your love will drive me mad at last;
this much is certain: love brings the lover strife.
It is the strand of your hair that has snared me so;
whatever befalls me, those scented locks bring it on.
If I could look at your rose of a face for one moment,
each look would bring a shining, radiant light.
Brow, eye and lash-point have joined forces to stir up trouble:
one shoots arrows, one draws a blade, each picks a fight.

passage.original:
وخريدة ألحاظها يسرعن في
قتل النفوس بطيئة الحركات
بانية الأعطاف كثبانة ال
أرداف هاروتية النظرات
قبلتها فنفعت حر جوانحي
بألذ من شهد بماء فرات
قالت وقد أنكرت ما فعلته بي
ألحاظها أنت الأبي العاتي
هزلاً تداعبني به ومنيتي
في الهزل من هاتيكم الكلمات

شرواك ألحاظ الجنبيات
passage.english:
And a maiden whose glances are quick
to kill souls, though her movements are slow:
a waist slender as a willow, hips heaped like sandhills,
eyes with the magic of Harut.
I kissed her, and cooled the fire in my ribs
with something sweeter than honey in sweet river water.
She said, when I complained of what her eyes
had done to me: “You are the stubborn, unruly one!”
She teased me with it in jest, and my heart's desire
lay in the jest of those words.
How many hardy men have been laid low before their time
by sidelong glances like these!

হাটে যায় রে নদ্যার চান কোনাকুনি পথ।
বাদ্যার ছেরি ডাক্যা বলে “কিন্যা আইন নথ”॥
বনের ফল তুইল্যা আনে দুইজনে খায়।
মালাম পাথরে দুইয়ে শুয়ে নিদ্রা যায়॥

Але расстацца нам час наступае;
Пэўна, ўжо доля такая у нас!
Моцна кахаў я цябе, дарагая, —
Але расстацца нам час.
Буду ў далёкім краю я нудзіцца,
Ў сэрцы любоў затаіўшы сваю,
Кожную ночку на зорку дзівіцца
Буду ў далёкім краю.
Глянь іншы раз на яе, у расстаньні,
Там з ёй зьліём мы пагляды свае…
Каб хоць на міг уваскрэсла каханьне,
Глянь іншы раз на яе…
passage.english:
But now the hour has come for us to part;
it must be that such is our lot!
I loved you deeply, my dear,
but the hour has come to part.
I will pine away in a far-off land,
keeping my love hidden in my heart;
every night I will gaze at the star,
there, in the far-off land.
Look at it sometimes while we're apart:
there our glances will meet as one…
So that our love may come alive for a moment,
look at it sometimes…

passage.original:
O la splendeur de notre joie,
Tissée en or dans l'air de soie !
Voici la maison douce et son pignon léger,
Et le jardin et le verger.
Voici le banc, sous les pommiers
D'où s'effeuille le printemps blanc,
A pétales frôlants et lents.
Voici des vols de lumineux ramiers
Plânant, ainsi que des présages,
Dans le ciel clair du paysage.
Voici — pareils à des baisers tombés sur terre
De la bouche du frêle azur —
Deux bleus étangs simples et purs,
Bordés naïvement de fleurs involontaires.
passage.english:
Oh, the splendour of our joy,
woven in gold into the silken air!
Here is the gentle house with its airy gable,
and the garden, and the orchard.
Here is the bench under the apple trees
where the white spring is shedding
its slow petals, brushing as they fall.
Here are flights of bright wood pigeons
gliding, like signs of what is to come,
in the clear sky above the land.
Here — like kisses dropped to earth
from the lips of the fragile blue —
are two blue ponds, plain and pure,
fringed artlessly with flowers no one planted.

passage.original:
Amor... ¿oísteis?... Amor... ¿Acaso
No veis cómo arde todo a su paso?
Amor de otoño que huye el ocaso.
Dejad, señora, que un breve instante
Pose mis labios, como un amante,
En el extremo de vuestro guante.
Como un amante que ve de hinojos
La maravilla de vuestros ojos,
De vuestros labios frescos y rojos;
Como un amante que fuera un niño
Que pide, en premio de su cariño,
La flor que adorna vuestro corpiño.
passage.english:
Love… did you hear? … Love… Do you not see
how everything burns where it goes?
Autumn love, fleeing the sunset.
Let me, my lady, for one brief moment
rest my lips, as a lover would,
on the very tip of your glove.
Like a lover who, on his knees, beholds
the marvel of your eyes,
of your lips, so fresh and red;
like a lover who was a child
asking, as the prize for his devotion,
for the flower that decks your bodice.

passage.original:
Sinoć, kad se vratih iz topla hamama,
Prođoh pokraj bašte staroga imama;
Kad tamo, u bašti, u hladu jasmina,
S ibrikom u ruci stajaše Emina.
Ja kakva je, pusta! Tako mi imana,
Stid je ne bi bilo da je kod sultana!
Pa još kad se šeće i plećima kreće...
- Ni hodžin mi zapis više pomoć neće!...
Ja joj nazvah selam. Al' moga mi dina,
Ne šće ni da čuje lijepa Emina,
No u srebren ibrik zahitila vode
Pa po bašti đule zalivati ode;
S grana vjetar duhnu pa niz pleći puste
Rasplete joj one pletenice guste,
passage.english:
Last night, coming home from the warm hammam,
I went past the old imam's garden;
and there, in the garden, in the jasmine's shade,
stood Emina with a jug in her hand.
And what a beauty! By my faith,
she'd be no shame even in the sultan's house!
And then, when she walks and her shoulders move…
not even the hodja's amulet can save me now!
I wished her peace. But, by my religion,
lovely Emina would not even hear it;
she just dipped water into her silver jug
and went off through the garden to water the roses;
a wind blew from the branches and, down her shoulders,
loosened those thick braids of hers,

passage.original:
“Ora (direis) ouvir estrelas! Certo
Perdeste o senso!” E eu vos direi, no entanto,
Que, para ouvi-las, muita vez desperto
E abro as janelas, pálido de espanto...
E conversamos toda a noite, enquanto
A via-láctea, como um pálio aberto,
Cintila. E, ao vir do sol, saudoso e em pranto,
Inda as procuro pelo céu deserto.
Direis agora: “Tresloucado amigo!
Que conversas com elas? Que sentido
Tem o que dizem, quando estão contigo?”
E eu vos direi: “Amai para entendê-las!
Pois só quem ama pode ter ouvido
Capaz de ouvir e de entender estrelas”.
passage.english:
“Listening to stars!” you'll say. “You must
have taken leave of your senses!” And yet I'll tell you
that often I wake up to listen to them
and fling the windows open, pale with awe…
And we talk the whole night through, while
the Milky Way, like a canopy spread open,
sparkles. And when the sun comes, missing them, in tears,
I still search for them across the empty sky.
Now you will say: “My poor deluded friend!
What do you talk about with them? What sense
is there in what they say when they're with you?”
And I will tell you: “Love, and you'll understand them!
For only someone who loves can have ears
able to hear and to understand the stars.”

passage.original:
Душата ми отново посети
и в есента Великден ми донесе!
И свeтъл звон в тъмата се разнесе, -
крило на херувим над нас лети.
И домът ми с дъхът си освети,
Раздигнаха се тъмните завеси,
и мъртва в мене радостта възкресе:
във нея бяхме само аз и ти.
В една целувка се души ни сляха,
и пролет цъфна, птичките запяха,
събудиха градинските цветя.
И във мълчанието от бяла свила,
загърнала ме твоята закрила,
на тихото й аз крило летя.
passage.english:
Once more you came to visit my soul
and brought me Easter in the autumn!
A bright chiming spread through the darkness,
a cherub's wing goes flying over us.
You filled my house with light by your breath;
the dark curtains were drawn back,
and the joy that had died in me rose again:
in it there were only you and me.
In one kiss our souls were joined,
and spring broke into flower, the birds began to sing
and woke the flowers of the garden.
And in the silence of white silk,
wrapped in your keeping,
I fly on its quiet wing.

passage.original:
Ca tem nada na es bida
Mas grande que amor
Se Deus ca tem medida
Amor inda é maior.
Maior que mar, que céu
Mas, entre tudo cretcheu
De meu inda é maior
Cretcheu más sabe,
É quel que é di meu
Ele é que é tchabe
Que abrim nha céu.
Cretcheu más sabe
É quel qui crem
Ai sim perdel
Morte dja bem
passage.english:
There is nothing in this life
Greater than love;
If God has no measure,
Love is greater still.
Greater than the sea, than the sky,
But, above all, my own beloved
Is greater still.
The sweetest beloved
Is the one who is mine;
They are the key
That opens my heaven.
The sweetest beloved
Is the one who loves me;
Ah, if I lost them,
Death would come.

passage.original:
Was it a year or lives ago
We took the grasses in our hands,
And caught the summer flying low
Over the waving meadow lands,
And held it there between our hands?
The while the river at our feet—
A drowsy inland meadow stream—
At set of sun the after-heat
Made running gold, and in the gleam
We freed our birch upon the stream.
There down along the elms at dusk
We lifted dripping blade to drift,
Through twilight scented fine like musk,
Where night and gloom awhile uplift,
Nor sunder soul and soul adrift.
passage.english:

Through twilight scented fine like musk,

passage.original:
靜女其姝，
俟我於城隅，
愛而不見，
搔首踟躕。
靜女其孌，
貽我彤管，
彤管有煒，
說懌女美。
自牧歸荑，
洵美且異，
匪女之為美，
美人之貽。
passage.english:
The quiet girl is lovely;
she waits for me at the corner of the city wall.
She hides and will not show herself;
I scratch my head and walk up and down.
The quiet girl is fair;
she gives me a red reed.
The red reed glows,
and I delight in how fine you are.
From the pastures she brings me a young shoot,
truly beautiful and rare.
It is not you, little shoot, that are beautiful:
you are the gift of a beautiful girl.

passage.original:
Oye: bajo las ruinas de mis pasiones,
y en el fondo de esta alma que ya no alegras,
entre polvos de ensueños y de ilusiones
yacen entumecidas mis flores negras.
Ellas son el recuerdo de aquellas horas
en que presa en mis brazos te adormecías,
mientras yo suspiraba por las auroras
de tus ojos, auroras que no eran mías.
Ellas son mis dolores, capullos hechos;
los intensos dolores que en mis entrañas
sepultan sus raíces, cual los helechos
en las húmedas grietas de las montañas.
passage.english:
Listen: under the ruins of my passions,
at the bottom of this soul you no longer make glad,
among the dust of daydreams and illusions,
my black flowers lie numbed.
They are the memory of those hours
when you fell asleep, held captive in my arms,
while I sighed for the dawns
of your eyes, dawns that were not mine.
They are my griefs, turned into buds:
the deep griefs that bury their roots
in my innermost self, like ferns
in the damp clefts of the mountains.

passage.original:
Desciende hasta el jardín, amada mía;
es hora en que las rosas y jazmines
inciensan a la tarde; en los confines
va cerrando sus párpados el día.
Anhelo de tus labios la ambrosía;
desciende hasta el jardín; los bandolines
alados ya no trinan; hay festines
de estrellas en la bóveda sombría.
La luna riega el ámbar de su lumbre
desde la comba inmensa de los cielos
y baja, hecha fulgor, hasta las pomas.
Como garza se eleva tras la cumbre
del monte, y el jazmín de mis anhelos
te invita a descender, con sus aromas.
passage.english:
Come down to the garden, my beloved;
It is the hour when the roses and jasmine
Perfume the evening like incense; at the edge of the sky
The day is closing its eyelids.
I long for the ambrosia of your lips;
Come down to the garden; the winged
Mandolins have stopped their trilling; there are feasts
Of stars in the darkening vault.
The moon pours out the amber of its light
From the immense curve of the heavens,
And comes down, turned to radiance, to the fruit trees.
Like a heron it rises behind the summit
Of the mountain, and the jasmine of my longing
Invites you, with its scent, to come down.

title: Utjeha kose (Consolation of Hair)
creator: Antun Gustav Matoš
editionDate: Linked digital transcription/facsimile; precise edition date not established
description: Sonnet in which the speaker dreams of a dead beloved and finds consolation in her still-living hair. Romantic love and mortality; tragic rather than celebratory.
provenance: Croatian original transcribed at Wikisource; Matica hrvatska confirms 1906 Savremenik publication; Croatian Encyclopedia confirms author and dates.
translation: Check transcription against a historical edition before final quotation; modern English translations have separate rights. Passage update (29 October 2026): Complete sonnet, 14 lines. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI); draft for editorial review.
rights: Original text: standard life-plus-70 term expired; author died 1914. Reuse assessment applies to the original words, not modern translations, editorial additions, musical settings or recordings. Publication-history and territorial exceptions are not universally assessed.

contextNote: Antun Gustav Matoš wrote this, his first sonnet, in Belgrade in 1906, while living in exile from Austria-Hungary after deserting from its army. He later returned to Zagreb and became the leading figure of Croatian modernism; this is still one of the best-known poems in the language.

passage.original:
Gledo sam te sinoć. U snu. Tužan. Mrtvu.
U dvorani kobnoj, u idili cvijeća,
Na visokom odru, u agoniji svijeća,
Gotov da ti predam život kao žrtvu.
Nisam plako. Nisam. Zapanjen sam stao
U dvorani kobnoj, punoj smrti krasne,
Sumnjajući da su tamne oči jasne
Odakle mi nekad bolji život sjao.
Sve baš, sve je mrtvo: oči dah i ruke,
Sve što očajanjem htjedoh da oživim
U slijepoj stravi i u strasti muke,
U dvorani kobnoj, mislima u sivim.
Samo kosa tvoja još je bila živa,
Pa mi reče: — Miruj! U smrti se sniva.
passage.english:
I saw you last night. In a dream. Sad. Dead.
In a fateful hall, in an idyll of flowers,
On a high bier, in the agony of candles,
Ready to give you my life as a sacrifice.
I did not weep. I did not. Stunned, I stood
In the fateful hall, full of beautiful death,
Doubting that those dark, clear eyes
Were where a better life once shone on me.
All, yes, all is dead: eyes, breath and hands,
All that in despair I longed to bring to life
In blind terror and in the passion of torment,
In the fateful hall, among grey thoughts.
Only your hair was still alive,
And it said to me: “Be still! In death one dreams.”

display.english: To Him — In the flattering dawn
display.creator: Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda

passage.original:
Volaban los años, y yo vanamente
Buscando seguía mi hermosa visión...
Mas dio al fin la hora; brillar vi tu frente,
Y «es él», dijo al punto mi fiel corazón.
Porque era, no hay duda, tu imagen querida,
-Que el alma inspirada logró adivinar-
Aquella que en alba feliz de mi vida
Miré para nunca poderla olvidar.
Por ti fue mi dulce suspiro primero;
Por ti mi constante, secreto anhelar
Y en balde el destino -mostrándose fiero-
Tendió entre nosotros las olas del mar.
passage.english:
The years flew by, and still, in vain,
I went on searching for my beautiful vision…
But at last the hour came; I saw your brow shine,
And “It is he,” my faithful heart said at once.
For it was, beyond doubt, your beloved image
— which my inspired soul had managed to divine —
The one I saw in the happy dawn of my life
And have never been able to forget.
For you was my first sweet sigh;
For you my constant, secret longing;
And in vain did fate, showing its cruelty,
Stretch the waves of the sea between us.

passage.original:
Διατί ποτέ μου δεν είδα ‘ξ αυτήσ σου
θάρος να λείψουν τα λαμπρά ‘που μένα,
τα ποια μου δώκεν το γλυκύν το δείσ σου
και δεν παύγουν ποτέ καιρόν κανέναν,
διατί δεν με ψηφά στην δούλεψήσ σου,
μισεύγω από την Κύπρον εις τα ξένα
αμμ’ έξευρε όπου πάγω, αγγέλισσά μου,
πάντα μ’ εσέν θέλ’ είσταιν η καρδιά μου.
passage.english:
Because I have never once seen in you
The courage to take from me the bright flames
That your sweet glance gave me,
And that never cease at any time,
Because you take no account of my devotion,
I am leaving Cyprus for foreign lands;
But know, wherever I go, my angel,
My heart will always be with you.

passage.original:
A ptáček jasnohlasý
mi odpovídá v písni:
Vím, jaká pečeť asi
ta zpěvná ústa tísní.
Vím, proč tak oněměly
rty dívčí v prostřed pění:
je uzamknul ret vřelý,
je stisklo políbení.
Když srdce k srdci sletí,
pak umlká a slyší
zpěv andělů jen pěti
tou sladkou němou tiší.
passage.english:
And a clear-voiced little bird
Answers me in song:
“I know what seal, it seems,
Is pressing on that singing mouth.
I know why the girl’s lips
Fell silent in mid-song:
Warm lips have locked them shut,
A kiss has pressed them closed.
When heart flies down to heart,
It falls quiet, and hears
Only the angels singing
In that sweet, wordless hush.”

passage.original:
Ven y tu mano del pecho amante
calme amorosa las penas mil,
¡oh de mis ansias único objeto!
Ven, que a ti sólo quiero en secreto
contar mis sueños de amor febril.
Mas no, que nunca mi amante anhelo
podré decirte libre de afán,
gimiendo a solas, en desconsuelo,
cual mis suspiros, en raudo vuelo,
mis ilusiones perdidas van.
Tuya es mi vida, tuya mi suerte,
de ti mi dicha pende o mi mal;
si al dolor quieres que venza fuerte,
sobre mi frente pálida vierte
de tu ternura todo el raudal.
passage.english:
Come, and let your hand, with love,
Ease the thousand sorrows of my loving breast,
O sole object of my longing!
Come, for to you alone I wish, in secret,
To tell my dreams of feverish love.
But no: never shall I be able
To tell you my loving longing free of fear;
Moaning alone, disconsolate,
Like my sighs, in swift flight,
My lost illusions slip away.
Yours is my life, yours my fate;
My joy or my sorrow hangs on you;
If you would have me overcome my pain,
Pour upon my pale brow
The whole flood of your tenderness.

title: El alma en los labios

Contains a suicidal declaration; not an uncomplicated positive-love choice. The selection is the original-language text; an existing English translation is not required. English passage: Earlier English draft by ChatGPT (replaced); draft for editorial review. Lines 5–16, three consecutive stanzas; opening and closing omitted. Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography. contextNote: Medardo Ángel Silva grew up poor in Guayaquil and belonged to the 'beheaded generation' of young Ecuadorian poets who died early. He died in 1919 aged 21; this poem, later a famous pasillo song, is shadowed by the despair in his life.

passage.original:
Porque mi pensamiento, lleno de este cariño
que en una hora feliz me hiciera esclavo tuyo,
Lejos de tus pupilas es triste como un niño
que se duerme soñando en tu acento de arrullo.
Para envolverte en besos quisiera ser el viento
y quisiera ser todo lo que tu mano toca;
ser tu sonrisa, ser hasta tu mismo aliento,
para poder estar más cerca de tu boca.
Vivo de tu palabra, y eternamente espero
llamarte mía, como quien espera un tesoro.
lejos de ti comprendo lo mucho que te quiero
y, besando tus cartas, ingenuamente lloro.
passage.english:
For my thoughts, full of this tenderness
that made me your slave in one happy hour,
are sad, away from your eyes, like a child
who falls asleep dreaming of the lull of your voice.
To wrap you in kisses I would like to be the wind,
and to be everything your hand touches;
to be your smile, to be your very breath,
so as to be closer to your mouth.
I live on your words, and forever hope
to call you mine, as one hopes for a treasure;
far from you I see how much I love you,
and, kissing your letters, I simply weep.

display.title: مضناك جفاه مرقده
display.english: Your lovesick one has been forsaken by sleep
display.creator: Ahmad Shawqi

passage.original:
مضناك جفاهُ مرقده
وبكاه ورحمَ عودُهُ
حيرانُ القلبِ مُعَذَّبُهُ
مقروح الجفنِ مسهده
أودى حرفاً إلا رمقاً
يُبقيه عليك وتُنْفِدهُ
يستهوي الورق تأوهه
ويذيب الصخرَ تنهدهُ
ويناجي النجمَ ويتعبه
ويُقيم الليلَ ويُقْعِدهُ
ويعلم كلَّ مطوقةٍ
شجناً في الدَّوحِ ترددهُ
كم مد لطيفكَ من شركٍ
وتأدب لا يتصيدهُ
فعساك بغُمْضٍ مُسعِفهُ
ولعلّ خيالك مسعدهُ
الحسنُ حَلَفْتُ بيُوسُفِهِ
والسورةِ إنك مفردهُ
قد وَدَّ جمالك أو قبساً
حوراءُ الخُلْدِ وأَمْرَدُه
passage.english:
Your lovesick one has been deserted by his bed,
and those who visit him weep and pity him.
His heart bewildered and tormented,
his eyelids sore, kept sleepless,
he has wasted to a thread, but for a last breath
that he keeps for you, and you use up.
His moaning draws the doves to him,
and his sighing melts the rock.
He confides in the stars and wears them out;
he keeps the night standing, and makes it sit.
He teaches every ring-necked dove
a sorrow to repeat among the trees.
How many snares he has set for your phantom,
yet, out of good manners, he does not trap it.
Perhaps you will grant him a moment’s sleep,
and perhaps your phantom will bring him joy.
I swear by beauty’s Joseph
and by his sura, that you are beauty’s only one.
The houris and the youths of paradise
have longed for your beauty, or even a spark of it.

Reuse assessment applies to the original words, not modern translations, editorial additions, musical settings or recordings. passage.original:
Vagar, soñando versos, en silentes caminos,
con la dorada lluvia del sol sobre tu frente;
y en un tronco sentados, mirarme largamente
en las dormidas aguas de tus ojos hialinos…
“Y qué linda”, dijeran al verte, campesinos
de esos que con sus vacas van buscando una fuente,
y yo: “Sus ojos miran, miran más dulcemente
que dos estrellas blancas en cielos vespertinos”.
Y tú te sonreirías sin vanidad ninguna;
después en nuestro rancho se entraría la luna
y ladraría al vernos, el perro blanco y fiel…
Como el café maduro fuera tu boca, mía,
y en el rancho con luna, mi boca bebería
en la flor de tus labios, un “te quiero” de miel.
passage.english:
To wander, dreaming verses, along silent paths,
With the golden rain of the sun upon your brow;
And, seated on a log, to gaze at myself at length
In the sleeping waters of your glassy eyes…
“And how lovely she is,” country people would say on seeing you,
The kind who go with their cows in search of a spring,
And I: “Her eyes look, they look more sweetly
Than two white stars in evening skies.”
And you would smile without the least vanity;
Then the moon would come into our farmhouse
And, seeing us, the white and faithful dog would bark…
Your mouth, mine, would be like ripe coffee,
And in the moonlit farmhouse my mouth would drink
From the flower of your lips a honeyed “I love you”.

passage.original:
Kaks selget silma mulle vaatnud
Kui taeva tähed südame,
Kaks selget silma põue saatnud
Mul täheläiget äkiste.
Kust oleks teadnud taganeda
Ma vaene vaga palgilta?
Nii peenet nägu põgeneda,
Nii selget silma süüdelda?
Et ühtepuhku mõttes suigun,
Et mõistus kõik mul metsa läind.
Et nagu unes ala tuigun:
Kaks selget silma seda teind!
passage.english:
Two clear eyes have looked into my heart
Like the stars of heaven,
Two clear eyes have sent into my breast
A sudden gleam of starlight.
How could I have known to turn away,
Poor, meek me, from that face?
To flee a face so fine,
To blame an eye so clear?
So that I keep drifting off in thought,
So that my wits have all gone astray,
So that I stumble about as in a dream:
Two clear eyes have done all this!

passage.original:
Mère des souvenirs, maîtresse des maîtresses,
O toi, tous mes plaisirs, ô toi, tous mes devoirs!
Tu te rappelleras la beauté des caresses,
La douceur du foyer et le charme des soirs,
Mère des souvenirs, maîtresse des maîtresses!
Les soirs illuminés par l'ardeur du charbon,
Et les soirs au balcon, voilés de vapeurs roses;
Que ton sein m'était doux! que ton cœur m'était bon!
Nous avons dit souvent d'impérissables choses
Les soirs illuminés par l'ardeur du charbon.
Que les soleils sont beaux dans les chaudes soirées!
Que l'espace est profond! que le cœur est puissant!
En me penchant vers toi, reine des adorées,
Je croyais respirer le parfum de ton sang.
Que les soleils sont beaux dans les chaudes soirées!
passage.english:
Mother of memories, loveliest of lovers,
you, all my pleasures, you, all my duties!
You'll remember the beauty of our caresses,
the softness of the hearth and the spell of the evenings,
mother of memories, loveliest of lovers!
Evenings lit by the glow of the coals,
and evenings on the balcony, veiled in pink haze;
how soft your breast was to me! how kind your heart!
Often we said things that will never die,
on evenings lit by the glow of the coals.
How beautiful the suns are on warm evenings!
How deep the sky is! How strong the heart!
Bending towards you, queen of the adored,
I seemed to breathe the perfume of your blood.
How beautiful the suns are on warm evenings!

So hold und schön und rein;
Ich schau dich an, und Wehmut

passage.original:
“Yes, I know that.
But this also I do know, that the gods are wont to make use of human instruments in approaching men.
The Infinite finds expression in the finite, and the ideal is realised in the actual.
And it has often occurred to me that the child-like hand that shall guide me through life’s labyrinthine ways is the self-same one that I now hold tenderly in my own.”
She began to understand.
She made an effort as if she would withdraw her hand.
She hesitated, and the next moment she surrendered the other also.
“You will be my teacher, then?” asked Kwamankra, half-persuasively, half-triumphantly.
“Yes,” she simply answered. “So may the gods of our race help me!”
As the days passed, the twain grew in that mutual understanding, the true basis of all happy unions.
Now and again he would tell her of his prospects, which he laughingly said were nil, having inherited little else beyond a clear head and a willing heart for work, with which he hoped they would be able to forge their way in life together;
to which Mansa would sweetly say that she wished she had a fortune to make things easy, but since she had it not, she would bring him the next best, a loyal heart and true, at which Kwamankra would chide her, and say that was the best of all.

κὤττι μοι μάλιστα θέλω γένεσθαι
μαινόλᾳ θύμῳ· τίνα δηὖτε Πείθω
μαῖς ἄγην ἐς σὰν φιλότατα, τίς σ', ὦ
Ψάπφ', ἀδικήει;
καὶ γὰρ αἰ φεύγει, ταχέως διώξει,
αἰ δὲ δῶρα μὴ δέκετ' ἀλλὰ δώσει,
αἰ δὲ μὴ φίλει, ταχέως φιλήσει
κωὐκ ἐθέλοισα.
ἔλθε μοι καὶ νῦν, χαλεπᾶν δὲ λῦσον
ἐκ μεριμνᾶν, ὄσσα δὲ μοι τελέσσαι
θῦμος ἰμέρρει, τέλεσον· σὺ δ' αὔτα
σύμμαχος ἔσσο.
passage.english:
And what I most wish to happen
For my maddened heart. “Whom now shall I persuade
To lead you back into her love? Who, O
Sappho, wrongs you?
For if she flees, soon she will pursue;
If she will not take gifts, she will give them;
And if she does not love, soon she will love,
Even against her will.”
Come to me now as well, and free me from harsh
Cares; all that my heart longs
To bring about, bring about; and you yourself
Be my ally.

passage.original:
En mi lóbrega y yerta fantasía
brilla tu imagen apacible y pura,
como el rayo de luz que el sol envía,
a través de una bóveda sombría
al roto mármol de una sepultura.
Callado, inerte, en estupor profundo,
mi corazón se embarga y se enajena,
y allá en su centro vibra moribundo
cuando entre el vano estrépito del mundo
la melodía de tu nombre suena.
Sin lucha, sin afán y sin lamento,
sin agitarme en ciego frenesí,
sin proferir un solo un leve acento,
las largas horas de la noche cuento,
¡Y pienso en ti…
passage.english:
In my gloomy, frozen imagination
Your image shines, peaceful and pure,
Like the ray of light the sun sends
Through a shadowed vault
Onto the broken marble of a tomb.
Silent, inert, in deep stupor,
My heart is seized and carried away,
And there, at its centre, it trembles, dying,
When, amid the empty clamour of the world,
The melody of your name is heard.
Without struggle, without striving, without lament,
Without stirring in blind frenzy,
Without uttering a single, faint sound,
I count the long hours of the night,
And think of you…

rights: Public-domain original in the UK and other life-plus-70 jurisdictions: author died 1906. Modern editorial additions and translations are separate.
source: Source text and provenance checked 28 October 2026.
contextNote: Oswald Durand was the most celebrated Haitian poet of his day, and he wrote Choucoune (1884) in Haitian Creole while in prison; set to music, it became a beloved song and later the English hit “Yellow Bird”. In the poem, Choucoune leaves the narrator for a white foreigner, a story that carried the weight of race and power in a country that had freed itself from French slavery in 1804.

passage.original:
Dériè gnou gras touff’ pingouin,
L’aut’jou, moin contré Choucoune ;
Li sourit, l’heur’li ouè moin,
Moin dit : « Ciel ! A là bell’ moune ! »
Li dit : « Ou trouvé ca cher ! »…
P’tits zoézeaux ta pé couté nous lan l’air…
Quand moin songé Ça, moin gangnin la peine,
Car dimpi jou-là, dé pieds moin lan chaîne !
Ca qui pis trist’lan tout ça,
Ca qui va surprendr’tout moune,
Cé ’pou ouè malgré temps-là,
Moin aimé toujours Choucoune !
passage.english:
Behind a thick clump of cactus,
The other day, I met Choucoune;
She smiled the moment she saw me,
I said: “Heavens! What a beautiful girl!”
She said: “You think so, dear?”…
Little birds were listening to us up in the air…
When I think of it, I am full of sorrow,
For since that day both my feet are in chains!
The saddest thing in all of this,
The thing that will surprise everyone,
Is to see that, in spite of it all,
I still love Choucoune!

passage.original:
לבבתני אחתי כלה
לבבתני באחד מעיניך
באחד ענק מצורניך
מה־יפו דדיך אחתי כלה
מה־טבו דדיך מיין
וריח שמניך מכל־בשמים
נפת תטפנה שפתותיך כלה
דבש וחלב תחת לשונך
וריח שלמתיך כריח לבנון
גן נעול אחתי כלה
גל נעול מעין חתום
passage.english:
You have taken my heart, my sister, my bride;
you have taken my heart with one of your eyes,
with one link of the chain about your neck.
How fair are your caresses, my sister, my bride!
How much finer your caresses than wine,
and the fragrance of your oils than all the spices!
Your lips let fall drops of honeycomb, my bride;
honey and milk lie beneath your tongue,
and the fragrance of your clothes is like the fragrance of Lebanon.
A garden barred is my sister, my bride,
a spring barred, a sealed fountain.

title: Sursum
creator: Juan Ramón Molina
editionDate: Linked digital transcription/facsimile; precise edition date not established
description: A sonnet promising that the lovers will remain together beyond death, their souls ascending united through the stars. A sustained affirmation of enduring romantic union.
provenance: Spanish Wikisource, “Súrsum”; UNAM biography confirms Honduran author 1875–1908.

Passage update (29 October 2026): Complete sonnet, 14 lines (Spanish Wikisource text, titled “Súrsum”). Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI); draft for editorial review.

Publication-history and territorial exceptions are not universally assessed. contextNote: Juan Ramón Molina was Honduras’s great modernist poet and a restless traveller across Central America, who knew Rubén Darío. He died in 1908, aged 33, and his poems were gathered after his death in Tierras, mares y cielos (1911).

passage.original:
Ya no nos separemos ni un momento,
porque –cuando se extingan nuestras vidas–
nuestras dos almas cruzarán unidas
el éter, en continuo ascendimiento.
Ajenas al humano sufrimiento,
de las innobles carnes desprendidas,
serán en una llama confundidas
en la región azúl del firmamento.
Sin dejar huellas ni visibles rastros,
más allá de la gloria de los astros,
entre auroras de eternos arreboles,
a obedecer iremos la divina
ley, fatal y suprema que domina
los espacios, las almas y los soles.
passage.english:
Let us not be parted even for a moment,
For, when our lives are extinguished,
Our two souls will cross together
Through the ether, rising for ever.
Strangers to human suffering,
Set free from ignoble flesh,
They will be merged into one flame
In the blue region of the firmament.
Leaving no traces or visible tracks,
Beyond the glory of the stars,
Among dawns of everlasting crimson clouds,
We will go to obey the divine
Law, fatal and supreme, that rules
The spaces, the souls and the suns.

title: Szeptember végén
creator: Sándor Petőfi
editionDate: Hungarian Wikisource transcription in the original spelling
description: Watching the first snow on the mountains, the young poet asks his wife whether she will marry again after his death, and promises to love her for ever.
provenance: Written at Koltó, September 1847; Hungarian Wikisource, original spelling.
translation: Work changed (30 October 2026): Margit Kaffka's “Szerettelek”, first printed in 1943, is replaced by a poem published in the poet's lifetime. Complete poem, 24 lines. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI); draft for editorial review.
rights: Public domain everywhere: Petőfi died 1849 and the poem was published in his lifetime.
source: Hungarian Wikisource: Szeptember végén
contextNote: Sándor Petőfi, Hungary's national poet, wrote this at Koltó in September 1847, on his honeymoon with Júlia Szendrey. Less than two years later he was killed fighting in the Hungarian revolution of 1848–49, aged 26, and Júlia did marry again.

passage.original:
Még nyílnak a völgyben a kerti virágok,
Még zöldel a nyárfa az ablak előtt,
De látod amottan a téli világot?
Már hó takará el a bérczi tetőt.
Még ifju szivemben a lángsugarú nyár
S még benne virít az egész kikelet,
De íme sötét hajam őszbe vegyűl már,
A tél dere már megüté fejemet.
Elhull a virág, eliramlik az élet...
Űlj, hitvesem, űlj az ölembe ide!
Ki most fejedet kebelemre tevéd le,
Holnap nem omolsz-e sirom fölibe?
Oh mondd: ha előbb halok el, tetemimre
Könnyezve borítasz-e szemfödelet?
S rábírhat-e majdan egy ifju szerelme,
Hogy elhagyod érte az én nevemet?
Ha eldobod egykor az özvegyi fátyolt,
Fejfámra sötét lobogóul akaszd,
Én feljövök érte a síri világból
Az éj közepén, s oda leviszem azt,
Letörleni véle könyűimet érted,
Ki könnyeden elfeledéd hivedet,
S e szív sebeit bekötözni, ki téged
Még akkor is, ott is, örökre szeret!
passage.english:
The garden flowers still bloom in the valley,
the poplar is still green before the window,
but do you see the winter world over there?
Snow already covers the mountain top.
The flame-bright summer still burns in my young heart,
and the whole of spring still blossoms there,
but look, my dark hair is turning grey,
the frost of winter has already touched my head.
The flower falls, and life runs on…
Sit, my wife, come sit here on my lap!
You who now lay your head upon my breast,
will you not fall tomorrow weeping on my grave?
Oh tell me: if I die first, will you
lay a shroud over my body, in tears?
And could the love of some young man persuade you
one day to give up my name for his?
If one day you throw off the widow's veil,
hang it on my grave-post like a dark flag;
I will come up for it from the world of the dead
at midnight, and take it down with me
to wipe away my tears for you,
who so lightly forgot the one who was true to you,
and to bind the wounds of this heart, which loves you
even then, even there, for ever!

title: Ferðalok (Journey’s End)
creator: Jónas Hallgrímsson
editionDate: Historical print edition; digital adaptation 2014
description: Recalls intimate companionship and asserts that eternity cannot divide souls that love one another.
provenance: Rit eftir Jónas Hallgrímsson, vol. I; National and University Library scan adapted by Project Runeberg in 2014

The selection is the original-language text; an existing English translation is not required. Passage update (29 October 2026): Final three stanzas, 18 lines, including the closing stanza. Runeberg’s OCR is unproofread; these lines read cleanly and are copied as printed. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI); draft for editorial review.

contextNote: Jónas Hallgrímsson was a poet and naturalist who helped renew Icelandic as a literary language while Iceland was ruled by Denmark. Ferðalok remembers a youthful journey with a girl he loved; it was published in 1845, the year he died in Copenhagen, aged 37.

passage.original:
Greiddi eg þér lokka
við Galtará
vel og vandlega;
brosa blómvarir,
blika sjónstjörnur,
roðnar heitur hlýr.
Fjær er nú fagurri
fylgd þinni
sveinn í djúpum dali;
ástarstjarna
yfir Hraundranga
skín á bak við ský.
Háa skilur hnetti
himingeimur,
blað skilur bakka og egg;
en anda, sem unnast,
fær aldregi
eilífð að skilið.
passage.english:
I combed your locks
By the river Galtará,
Well and with care;
Your flower-lips smile,
Your eye-stars shine,
Your warm cheek blushes.
Far now from your fair
Company
Is a young man in a deep valley;
The star of love
Above Hraundrangi
Shines behind the clouds.
Heaven’s vast space
Divides the high spheres,
A blade divides back and edge;
But spirits that love each other
Can never
Be parted by eternity.

title: অনন্ত প্রেম / Ananta Prem
creator: Rabindranath Tagore
originalDate: 2 Bhadra 1296 (August 1889), Jorasanko, Calcutta; collected in Manasi (1890)
editionDate: Sanchayita; Bengali Wikisource proofread transcription
description: The speaker feels he has loved the beloved in countless forms across lifetimes; every love and every poet’s song meets in this one love.
provenance: Manasi (1890); text from Sanchayita, printed p. 96, proofread on Bengali Wikisource
translation: Author translation; preface notes abridgement and paraphrase. Modern translations are separate. English passage: Original English text; not a translation. Poem 16, first three paragraphs; author’s English version, reflowed into 12 reading lines. Corrected obvious transcription in→is before unfinished; no new translation.. Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography. Work changed (29 October 2026): The Gardener, poem 16 (Tagore’s own English) replaced by the Bengali original অনন্ত প্রেম, whose source is certain. Complete poem, 20 lines. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI); draft for editorial review. Revision (30 October 2026): lines 1, 2 and 5 reworded so they do not echo the wording of published English versions.
rights: Public-domain original: Tagore died 1941, beyond the standard life-plus-70 term. Modern translations are separate.
source: Bengali Wikisource, Sanchayita: অনন্ত প্রেম
contextNote: Tagore wrote this poem in Calcutta in 1889, in his late twenties, and published it in Manasi (1890), the collection that established him as a major Bengali poet. In 1913 he became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature; he wrote under British rule, and in 1919 gave up his British knighthood in protest at the Amritsar massacre.

passage.original:
তোমারেই যেন ভালোবাসিয়াছি শত রূপে শতবার
জনমে জনমে যুগে যুগে অনিবার।
চিরকাল ধরে মুগ্ধ হৃদয় গাঁথিয়াছে গীতহার—
কত রূপ ধরে পরেছ গলায়, নিয়েছ সে উপহার
জনমে জনমে যুগে যুগে অনিবার।
যত শুনি সেই অতীত কাহিনী, প্রাচীন প্রেমের ব্যথা,
অতি পুরাতন বিরহমিলনকথা,
অসীম অতীতে চাহিতে চাহিতে দেখা দেয় অবশেষে
কালের তিমিররজনী ভেদিয়া তোমারি মুরতি এসে
চিরস্মৃতিময়ী ধ্রুবতারকার বেশে।
আমরা দুজনে ভাসিয়া এসেছি যুগলপ্রেমের স্রোতে
অনাদি কালের হৃদয়-উৎস হতে।
আমরা দুজনে করিয়াছি খেলা কোটি প্রেমিকের মাঝে
বিরহবিধুর নয়নসলিলে, মিলনমধুর লাজে—
পুরাতন প্রেম নিত্যনূতন সাজে।
আজি সেই চির-দিবসের প্রেম অবসান লভিয়াছে
রাশি রাশি হয়ে তোমার পায়ের কাছে।
নিখিলের সুখ, নিখিলের দুখ, নিখিল প্রাণের প্রীতি—
একটি প্রেমের মাঝারে মিশেছে সকল প্রেমের স্মৃতি
সকল কালের সকল কবির গীতি।
passage.english:
It is as if I have loved you, only you, in a hundred shapes, a hundred times,
birth upon birth, era upon era, without cease.
Forever my spellbound heart has strung a garland of songs;
In how many forms you have worn it round your neck and taken the gift,
birth upon birth, era upon era, without cease.
Whenever I hear those tales of the past, the ache of ancient love,
The age-old stories of parting and meeting,
As I gaze and gaze into the boundless past, at last
Your image appears, piercing the dark night of time,
In the guise of the pole star, remembered for ever.
We two have come floating on the stream of a love for two,
From the heart’s spring of time without beginning.
We two have played among millions of lovers,
In the tears of eyes grieving at parting, in the sweet shyness of meeting:
An old love in ever-new array.
Today that love of all our days has found its fulfilment,
Heaped up in abundance at your feet.
The joy of the whole world, its sorrow, the love of every living soul,
The memory of every love has mingled in this one love,
And the songs of every poet of every age.

passage.original:
Kupatah tangkai kusuma kukucup
Kendati mencari wangi asli
Cempaka tinggal tergulai lampai
Sayang tanganku hendak mencapai.
Teja! hanya cempaka ditayang daun
Aneka bunga menutup bumi
Impian lama datang mengalun
Kerana kusuma kenangan diri.
Harum rambutmu terasa ada
Dalam bunga duduk tersembunyi
Suma mana ratna mulia
Kanda sibuk tengah mencari
Pohon rendah dinaungi kemuning
Puteri dilindungi payung kembang
Bunga adinda kencana ramping
Irama kusuma abang seorang.
Wangi tertebar membawaku ragu
Mengambang abang ke hari lampau
Harum sepadan wangi rambutmu
Kalau terurai kita bergurau.
Melur! Duta rindu di purnama-raya
Kawan sendu di sunyi malam
Ratna rupa di hulu kemala
Penambah manis jiwa pendiam.
passage.english:
I break off a flower’s stem and kiss it,
Though it is the true fragrance I am seeking;
The champak hangs, drooping and slender,
Alas, my hand longs to reach it.
Evening glow! only the champak is cradled by leaves,
Flowers of every kind cover the earth;
An old dream comes drifting back
Because of the flower of my own memory.
The fragrance of your hair I can sense
Sitting hidden within the flowers;
Which flower is the noble jewel
That I, your lover, am busy searching for?
A low tree shaded by kemuning,
A princess sheltered by a parasol of blossom;
My darling’s flower, slender and golden,
The flower song of your lover alone.
The scattered scent fills me with doubt,
Your lover drifts back to days gone by;
A fragrance equal to the scent of your hair
When it was loosened and we laughed and teased.
Jasmine! Envoy of longing under the full moon,
Companion in sorrow in the silent night,
Jewel in form at the crown of gems,
Sweetening a quiet soul.

title: اگر آن ترک شیرازی / Agar an Turk-e Shirazi
creator: Hafez
editionDate: Persian text: Ganjoor online edition
description: Praise of the beloved in a ghazal.

Passage update (29 October 2026): Complete ghazal, 9 couplets (18 half-lines). Persian text from Ganjoor (ghazal 3), with Ganjoor’s added short-vowel marks removed; the letters are unchanged. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI); draft for editorial review. Revision (30 October 2026): retranslated from the Persian for the anthology review so that no line follows the wording of an earlier English version. Revision (30 October 2026, sensitivity review): lūliyān (line 5) translated as 'wandering minstrel girls' rather than with an ethnic slur.
rights: Original text: 14th-century poem, public domain. New English translation from the Persian; Gertrude Bell's 1897 translation is not used. Anthology review (30 October 2026): the poet died centuries ago and the poem was in print long before 1989, so it is public domain in the UK, EU and US; the online text is a transcription of a historical text, with no new authorship.

contextNote: Hafez lived in Shiraz in the fourteenth century and is the best-loved poet in Persian; families across Iran still keep his Divan at home and open it at random for guidance. Legend says Timur, conqueror of Samarkand and Bukhara, summoned Hafez to ask how he dared give those cities away for a mole.

display.title: اگر آن ترک شیرازی / Agar an Turk-e Shirazi
display.creator: Hafez

passage.original:
اگر آن ترک شیرازی به‌ دست‌ آرد دل ما را
به خال هندویش بخشم سمرقند و بخارا را
بده ساقی می باقی که در جنت نخواهی یافت
کنار آب رکناباد و گل‌گشت مصلا را
فغان! کاین لولیان شوخ شیرین‌کار شهرآشوب
چنان بردند صبر از دل که ترکان خوان یغما را
ز عشق ناتمام ما جمال یار مستغنی‌ است
به آب و رنگ و خال و خط چه حاجت روی زیبا را؟
من از آن حسن روزافزون که یوسف داشت دانستم
که عشق از پردهٔ عصمت برون آرد زلیخا را
اگر دشنام فرمایی و گر نفرین دعا گویم
جواب تلخ می‌زیبد لب لعل شکرخا را
نصیحت گوش کن جانا که از جان دوست‌تر دارند
جوانان سعادتمند پند پیر دانا را
حدیث از مطرب و می گو و راز دهر کمتر جو
که کس نگشود و نگشاید به حکمت این معما را
غزل گفتی و در سفتی بیا و خوش بخوان حافظ
که بر نظم تو افشاند فلک عقد ثریا را
passage.english:
If that Turk of Shiraz would only take my heart in hand,
for the dark mole on that cheek I'd give up Samarkand and Bukhara.
Bring the last of the wine, cupbearer: in paradise you won't find
the banks of the Ruknabad or the flowered paths of Musalla.
Ah, these playful wandering minstrel girls, so charming, such trouble to the town,
have stripped the patience from my heart as Turks strip a table of its spoils.
My love is incomplete, but my beloved's beauty does not need it:
a lovely face has no use for powder, colour, beauty-spot or pencil.
From that beauty of Joseph's, growing day by day, I learned
how love draws Zulaikha out from behind the curtain of virtue.
Abuse me if you like, curse me: I'll pray for you all the same;
a bitter answer becomes a ruby lip that rains down sugar.
Take some advice, my dear: young people blessed by fortune
love the counsel of a wise old man more than life itself.
Talk of minstrels and wine, and don't dig into the world's secret,
for no one has solved this riddle by wisdom, and no one will.
You've made your ghazal and pierced your pearls; come, Hafez, sing it well,
for the sky scatters the string of the Pleiades over your verse.

display.english: Layla smiled at me from her balcony
display.creator: Jamil Sidqi al-Zahawi

passage.original:
تَبَسَّمت ليَ لَيلى فَوقَ شرفتها
كَما تَبَسَّمَ في أَفنانِه الزَهَرُ
لَقَد كلفت بها سَمراء فاتنة
في جيدها تلع في عينها حَوَرُ
قَدٌّ كَما شاءَت الأهواء معتدلٌ
ما شانه زارياً طولٌ وَلا قِصَرُ
إذا مَشَت تَتَثنّى عند مشيتها
كَما تَمايل غُصنٌ ناعم غضر
لَيلى لأَنتِ منَى نفسي وَحاجتها
وأنتَ وحدك يا لَيلى لها الوطر
passage.english:
Layla smiled at me from her balcony,
as blossom smiles among its branches.
I have fallen for her, a bewitching dark beauty,
with a long, graceful neck and eyes of deep contrast.
Her figure is just as desire would wish it,
marred by neither too much height nor too little.
When she walks, she sways as she goes,
like a soft, fresh branch bending.
Layla, you are my soul’s wish and its need,
and you alone, Layla, are its desire.

title: When You Are Old
creator: W. B. Yeats
editionDate: Undated Academy of American Poets transcription

Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography.

contextNote: Yeats wrote this for Maud Gonne, the actor and revolutionary he loved for years and who turned down his proposals. It belongs to the Irish literary revival, when writers set out to build a national culture while Ireland was still under British rule.

passage.original:
When you are old and grey and full of sleep,
And nodding by the fire, take down this book,
And slowly read, and dream of the soft look
Your eyes had once, and of their shadows deep;
How many loved your moments of glad grace,
And loved your beauty with love false or true,
But one man loved the pilgrim soul in you,
And loved the sorrows of your changing face;
And bending down beside the glowing bars,
Murmur, a little sadly, how Love fled
And paced upon the mountains overhead
And hid his face amid a crowd of stars.

passage.original:
מי אתה? מדוע יד מושטת
לא פוגשת יד אחות?
ועינים אך תמתנה רגע
והנה שפלו כבר נבוכות.
גן נעול. לא שביל אליו, לא דרך.
גן נעול - אדם.
האלך לי? או אכה בסלע
עד זוב דם?
passage.english:
Who are you? Why does a hand held out
not meet a sister's hand?
And eyes wait only a moment,
and look, they're already lowered in confusion.
A locked garden. No path to it, no way in.
A locked garden: a person.
Shall I go away? Or beat against the rock
till the blood runs?

passage.original:
Tanto gentile e tanto onesta pare
La donna mia, quand’ella altrui saluta,
Ch’ogni lingua divien tremando muta,
E gli occhi non l’ardiscon di guardare.
Ella sen va, sentendosi laudare,
Benignamente d’umiltà vestuta;
E par che sia una cosa venuta
Di cielo in terra a miracol mostrare.
Mostrasi sì piacente a chi la mira,
Che dà per gli occhi una dolcezza al core,
Che intender non la può chi non la prova.
E par che della sua labbia si muova
Un spirito soave e pien d’amore,
Che va dicendo all’anima: ‘sospira.’
passage.english:
So gracious and so modest does she seem,
my lady, when she greets anyone,
that every tongue trembles and goes mute,
and eyes do not dare to look at her.
She passes, hearing people praise her,
kindly, dressed in humility,
and seems to be a thing that came
from heaven down to earth to show a wonder.
She seems so pleasing to whoever looks at her
that through the eyes she sends a sweetness to the heart
which no one can understand who has not felt it;
and from her lips there seems to come
a gentle spirit full of love
that keeps on saying to the soul: “Sigh.”

title: A Red Flower
creator: Claude McKay
editionDate: 1922 base collection; university edition 2022
description: Sensual admiration of the beloved through flower, bee and kiss imagery.

passage.original:
Your lips are like a southern lily red,
Wet with the soft rain-kisses of the night,
In which the brown bee buries deep its head,
When still the dawn’s a silver sea of light.
Your lips betray the secret of your soul,
The dark delicious essence that is you,
A mystery of life, the flaming goal
I seek through mazy pathways strange and new.
Your lips are the red symbol of a dream.
What visions of warm lilies they impart,
That line the green bank of a fair blue stream,
With butterflies and bees close to each heart!

passage.original:
しのぶれど
色に出でにけり
わが恋は
物や思ふと
人の問ふまで
passage.english:
I hid it, and yet
it has come into my face,
this love of mine,
so that people ask me,
“Is something on your mind?”

title: عتبت سلمى علينا سفاها
creator: al-Walid ibn Yazid (al-Walid II)
editionDate: Kitab al-Aghani (first printed Bulaq, 1868), vol. 7
description: Salma is angry because the poet has insulted her father; he swears that he meant her no harm, that she fills his earth and sky, and that he will keep apologising until she forgives him.

Complete poem, 6 couplets. Fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI) made directly from the original; draft for editorial review.

contextNote: Al-Walid II spent much of his life at the Umayyad desert palaces of the Balqa, in today's Jordan, before becoming caliph in 743; he was killed a year later. His songs to Salma, whom he married after long courting her, were set to music by his court singers and preserved in the 10th-century Book of Songs.

passage.original:
عَتَبَت سَلمى عَلَينا سَفاها
أَن سَبَبتُ اليَومَ فيها أَباها
كانَ حَقُّ العَتبِ يا قَومُ مِنّي
لَيسَ مِنها كانَ قَلبي فِداها
فَلَئِن كُنتُ أَرَدتُ بِقَلبي
لِأَبي سَلمى خِلافَ هَواها
فَثَكِلتُ اليَومَ سَلمى فَسَلمى
مَلَأَت أَرضي مَعاً وَسَماها
غَيرَ أَنّي لا أَظُنُّ عَدُوّاً
قَد أَتاها كاشِحاً بِأَذاها
فَلَها العُتبى لَدَينا وَقَلَّت
أَبَداً حَتّى أَنالَ رِضاها
passage.english:
Salma reproached me, rashly,
because today, over her, I insulted her father.
By rights, my friends, the reproach should be mine,
not hers; and still my heart would be her ransom.
If ever in my heart I wished
Salma's father anything against her will,
then may I lose Salma this very day: Salma,
who fills my earth and my sky together.
Still, I cannot believe that some enemy
has gone to her in spite, to do her harm;
so she shall have my apology, though it is little,
for ever, until I win her favour.

passage.original:
Көзімнің қарасы,
Көңілімнің санасы,
Бітпейді іштегі,
Ғашықтық жарасы.
Қазақтың данасы,
Жасы үлкен ағасы.
Бар демес сендей бір
Адамның баласы.
Жылайын, жырлайын,
Ағызып көз майын.
Айтуға келгенде,
Қалқама сөз дайын.
Жүректен қозғайын,
Әдептен озбайын.
Өзі де білмей ме,
Көп сөйлеп созбайын.
Тереңдеп қарайсың,
Телміріп тұрмайсың.
Бихабар жүргенсіп,
Бек қатты сынайсың.
passage.english:
Pupil of my eye,
Thought of my heart,
The wound of love within me
Never heals.
Neither the wisest of the Kazakhs
Nor the eldest of their elders
Would say there exists one
Among the children of men like you.
Let me weep, let me sing,
Letting my tears stream down.
When it comes to speaking,
I have words ready for my darling.
Let me stir them from my heart
And not overstep good manners.
Does she not know it herself?
Let me not drag it out with too many words.
You look at me deeply,
Yet you do not stand gazing with longing.
Pretending to know nothing,
You test me very hard.

passage.original:
إن هنداً يرقُّ منها المحيّا
ليس إلا من الحّيا أن تُحَيّا
رَبِّ هبْ لي من الجلادة صبراً
آتني من لدنْكَ ربِّ وَلِيّا
لا تَذْرني من الكآبة والوَجْ
دِ إلهي أهيم فرداً خليّا
كيف أنسى كلامَها اليومَ لما
نبذتْني به مكاناً قصيّا
عاتبتْني فأوسعتْني عِتاباً
فكأني أتيتُ شيئاً فريّا
ذاتُ قْرُطٍ كأنه النجمُ هندٌ
ووشاحٍ إذا انبرتْ كالثريّا
passage.english:
Hind, whose face grows tender
Only from shyness when she is greeted —
Lord, grant me patience to endure;
Give me, Lord, a helper from Your presence.
Do not leave me, out of sorrow and long-
ing, my God, to wander alone and forsaken.
How can I forget her words today, when
With them she cast me off to a distant place?
She reproached me, and reproached me at length,
As if I had done something unheard of.
Hind, with an earring like a star,
And a sash that, when she sets out, is like the Pleiades.

passage.original:
Ikkatra mana jūta
Pie Tevim vien grib traukt,
Kā ziedonī man krūtīs
Viss cenšas zaļot, plaukt.
Tur uzzied balti ziedi
Un ugunssarkani,
No kupluma un smaržas
Tie līkst kā reibuši.
Un visas manas dziesmas
Ap tiem kā bites dūc
Un, viņās nogrimdamas,
Sev saldu medu sūc.
passage.english:
Every feeling of mine
Longs to rush to you alone,
As in springtime, in my breast,
Everything strives to turn green and bloom.
There white flowers open,
And fire-red ones,
Heavy with fullness and fragrance
They bend as if drunk.
And all my songs
Hum around them like bees
And, sinking into them,
Suck sweet honey for themselves.

passage.original:
“Well, when this had gone on over two years, one evening about twilight, when I had finished my work, I went and sat under the cola-tree behind our house and pretended to be stringing my beads;
But my true object was soon realized.
Momo soon joined me and sat down by my side.
Who can picture our feelings as that evening we sat beneath the shadows of that stately cola, in the clear moonlight?
We sat side by side on the green grass, talking little nothings.
By and by he took a long breath, somehow I felt anxious just because of that sigh.
He then took both my hands in his, sending a thrill clean through me.
Planting his frank, honest eyes on mine which soon were directed to the ground, he said: ‘Guanya Pau, nah Edear (I love you); ya in dear wah?’ (Do you love me?)
What could I say but to whisper faintly: ‘Da keker’ (with all my heart).

passage.original:
أسير هواك لا يرجو سراحا
ولا يلتذّ بعد لماك راحا
وقد طال المطال فليت شعري
أيحسن أن يقول الناس باحا
وما سلّمت مذ حرّمت وصلي
فكيف تحرم النظر المباحا
بروحي فاتر الألحاظ أحوى
بكسر جفونه مزج المزاحا
يصول على الفؤاد بها صحاحاً
ويثخن كسرها قلبي جراحا
passage.english:
The captive of your love hopes for no release,
And, after your lips, takes no pleasure in wine.
The waiting has grown long; I wish I knew
Whether it would be right for people to say he has told his secret.
You have not greeted me since you forbade our meeting;
So how can you forbid even the glance that is allowed?
My life for the one with languid glances and dark lips,
Who mixes teasing into the droop of their eyelids:
With those glances, still whole, they assail my heart,
And their drooping covers my heart with wounds.

passage.original:
Be bažnyčios, be altorių,
Be sumainymo žiedų...
Žirgai skrenda, kiek tik nori,
Skrendam, lekiam vienu du!
Balti vėjai plaukus glosto
Jau toli žmonių garsai –
Iš auksinio žvaigždžių sosto
Štai, mus laimina Jisai!
Jis, kurs davė žmogui širdį
Su troškimais neramiais,
Vasaros vynu nugirdė –
Jis ir nuodėmes atleis!
Be bažnyčios, be altorių...
Žirgai lekia žvengdami –
Lekia, lekia musų norai
Nesulaikomi, jauni!
passage.english:
Without a church, without altars,
Without exchanging rings…
The horses fly as far as they please,
We fly, we race, just the two of us!
White winds stroke our hair,
The voices of people are already far away —
From the golden throne of the stars,
Look, He is blessing us!
He who gave the human heart
Its restless longings,
And made it drunk on summer wine —
He will forgive our sins as well!
Without a church, without altars…
The horses race on, neighing —
Our desires race, race on,
Unstoppable and young!

Buloh perindu di-atas atap,
Hendak di-buat bambu joran;
Kalau rindu jangan meratap,
Siapa lalu baik di-pesan.
Anak balam di-atas panggong,
Kalau tuan ka-Bandar Rekan;

passage.original:
Min kellu jgħidli, ja miskin jiena,
Li dal-mant f'qalbi jien kelli nġib!
U l-ebda fejda u l-ebda ħniena
Fl-imħabba tiegħi ma kelli nsib!
Qanpiena mbierka! fejn dari ħossok
Ikabbar fija kien qalb u ruħ;
Tħassarli 'l qalbi daż-żmien inħossok,
Il-ħabta tiegħek tiġbidli d-dmugħ!
Lilek nistħajjel nilmaħ quddiemi
Kull fejn f'għajnejja nara s-sabiħ;
Fuqek għall-ajru inxerred kliemi
Leħnek nistħajjel nisma' mar-riħ.
U f'dit-taqriqa qalbi tithenna
Iżda t-taqriqa fija ma ddum;
L-uġigħ urajha qalbi tistenna
Bil-qawwa tiegħu taqa' u ma tqum.
passage.english:
Who could have told me, poor me,
that I would carry this mantle of grief in my heart,
and that no comfort and no mercy
would I find in my love!
Blessed bell! where once, hearing you,
my heart and soul would swell within me,
now hearing you breaks my heart;
your tolling draws my tears!
I imagine I glimpse you before me
wherever my eyes see beauty;
I scatter my words about you to the air,
I imagine I hear your voice on the wind.
And in this rapture my heart takes comfort,
but the rapture does not stay with me;
after it my heart awaits the pain,
and under its force falls and does not rise.

display.title: Esta tarde, mi bien
display.creator: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

passage.original:
Esta tarde, mi bien, cuando te hablaba,
como en tu rostro y tus acciones vía
que con palabras no te persuadía,
que el corazón me vieses deseaba;
y Amor, que mis intentos ayudaba,
venció lo que imposible parecía:
pues entre el llanto, que el dolor vertía,
el corazón deshecho destilaba.
Baste ya de rigores, mi bien, baste:
no te atormenten más celos tiranos,
ni el vil recelo tu inquietud contraste
con sombras necias, con indicios vanos,
pues ya en líquido humor viste y tocaste
mi corazón deshecho entre tus manos.
passage.english:
This evening, my love, as I spoke with you,
since I could see from your face and what you did
that my words were not convincing you,
I wished that you could see my heart;
and Love, who was helping my attempt,
achieved what seemed impossible:
for in the tears that grief was shedding
my heart, undone, was flowing out.
Enough of harshness now, my love, enough:
let tyrant jealousy torment you no more,
nor let base suspicion trouble your peace
with foolish shadows and with empty signs,
since you have seen and touched, as liquid,
my heart, undone, between your hands.

passage.original:
A fost odată ca-n povești,
A fost ca niciodată,
Din rude mari împărătești,
O prea frumoasă fată.
Și era una la părinți
Și mândră-n toate cele,
Cum e Fecioara între sfinți
Și luna între stele.
Din umbra falnicelor bolți
Ea pasul și-l îndreaptă
Lângă fereastră, unde-n colț
Luceafărul așteaptă.
Privea în zare cum pe mări
Răsare și străluce,
Pe mișcătoarele cărări
Corăbii negre duce.
Îl vede azi, îl vede mâni,
Astfel dorința-i gata;
El iar, privind de săptămâni,
Îi cade dragă fata.
Cum ea pe coate-și răzima
Visând ale ei tâmple
De dorul lui și inima
Și sufletu-i se împle.
Și cât de viu s-aprinde el
În orișicare sară,
Spre umbra negrului castel
Când ea o să-i apară.
passage.english:
Once upon a time, as in the tales,
as never was before,
of great imperial lineage
there lived a lovely girl.
She was her parents’ only child,
and proud in everything,
as is the Virgin among saints
and the moon among the stars.
From the shadow of the lofty vaults
she turns her steps
to the window, where in a corner
the Evening Star is waiting.
She watched how, far away on the seas,
he rises and shines,
and on the moving paths
guides the black ships.
She sees him today, she sees him tomorrow,
and so her longing is born;
and he, gazing at her for weeks,
falls in love with the girl.
As she leaned on her elbows,
resting her temples, dreaming,
her heart and soul
are filled with longing for him.
And how brightly he flares up
every evening
towards the shadow of the black castle
when she appears to him.

passage.original:
Үлэмжийн чанар төгөлдөр
Өнгө тунамал толь шиг
Үзэсгэлэнтэй царайг чинь үзвээс
Өнгө лагшин төгөлдөр өө
Үнэхээр сэтгэлийг булаана.
Хөшүүн сэтгэлийг уяруулагч
Хөхөө шувууны эгшиг шиг
Хөөрхөн эелдэг ааш чинь
Хөгжиж суухад урамтай
Хөөрхөн аальт минь зээ.
Учирмагц сэнгэнэсэн
Уран гол шиг бие чинь
Угаас хамт бүтсэн
Улаан зандны үнэр шиг
Улам сэтгэлийг хөдөлгөнө.
Бадмын дундаас дэлгэрсэн
Балын амттай адил
Баясгалантай биеийг чинь үзвээс
Бахдаж ханашгүй
Баярыг улам арвитгана.
Хүний энэхэн насанд
Хүссэн хэргээ бүтээгээд
Хүсэлт тэнгэрийн оронд
Хөлгүй жаргалангийн дунд
Хөвөн цэнгэн жаргая.
passage.english:
Perfect in every noble quality,
clear-coloured as a mirror:
when I see your lovely face,
your form so perfect, oh,
it truly captivates my heart.
Softening even a hardened heart,
like the song of the cuckoo,
your sweet and gentle ways
make it a joy to sit with you,
my lovely one with your charming ways.
The moment we meet, refreshing
as a lovely river, your body,
like the scent of red sandalwood
born with it from the start,
stirs my heart ever more.
Like the taste of honey
spread from the heart of the lotus,
when I see your joyful self,
I cannot have my fill of admiring you,
and my joy grows ever greater.
In this one human life,
having done what we long to do,
in the heaven of our wishes,
amid boundless bliss,
let us float in delight together.

passage.original:
Док ево ти дивне виле лаким кроком ђе ми лети –
завид’те ми, сви бесмртни, на тренутак овај свети!
Ход је вилин млого дични на Аврорин када шеће,
од сребрног свога прага над прољећем кад се креће;
зрак је виле младолике тако красан ка Атине,
огледало и мазање презиру јој черте фине.
Устав’ луно, б’јела кола, продужи ми часе миле,
кад су сунце над Инопом уставити могле виле.
Прелесницу како видим, загрлим је ка бог вели,
уведем је под шатором к испуњењу светој жељи.
При зракама красне луне, при свјећици запаљеној
пламена се споји душа ка душици раскаљеној
и цјеливи божествени душу с душом драгом слију.
Ах, цјеливи, божа мана, све прелести рајске лију!
Цјелителни балсам свети најмирисни аромати
што је небо земљи дало на усне јој стах сисати.
Совршенство творенија, таинствене силе боже,
ништа љепше нит’ је када нити од ње створит може!
passage.english:
When look, a lovely fairy comes flying to me with a light step —
envy me, all you immortals, this holy moment!
The fairy’s step is far more stately than Aurora’s when she walks
from her silver threshold as she moves above the spring;
the gaze of the youthful fairy is as lovely as Athena’s,
her fine features scorn both mirror and paint.
Stay, moon, your white chariot; prolong my precious hours,
since fairies once could make the sun stand still above Inop.
As soon as I see the enchantress, I embrace her as a god would,
and lead her into the tent to fulfil a holy wish.
By the rays of the lovely moon, by a lighted candle,
a soul of flame joined a soul aglow,
and divine kisses poured soul into beloved soul.
Ah, kisses, manna of God, pouring out all the charms of heaven!
The holy healing balm, the most fragrant of perfumes
that heaven gave the earth, I began to drink from her lips.
Perfection of creation, mysterious power of God,
nothing more beautiful ever was, or could be made, than she!

passage.original:
هَل لِصَبٍّ مِن لَماكَ المُزدَري
بِسُلافِ الراح
رَشَفاتٌ مُزِجَت بِالسُكرِ
تَمنَحُ الأَفراح
مَروِيّاتٌ عَن صَحاحِ الجَوهَرِ
عَن مُنى الأَرواح
عَن هِلالِ الحُسنِ عَن ظُبى النَقا
عَن قَضيبِ البان
مِن جِنانَ الوَصلِ دوني أَغلَفا
رَقَّ يا رَضوان
وَاِرثِ لي مِن ذا العَذابِ الأَكبَرِ
فَعَسى أَرتاح
فَعَلى ذاكَ المُحَيّا الأَنوارِ
ذي السَنا الوَضّاح
مِن شَجٍّ نَشرُ سَلامٍ عَنبَري
ما اِنبَرى الإِصباح
وَثَنَت بانَ الرُبى كَفُّ الصَبا
وَشَدا القُمري
وَصَبا قَلبي لِأَيّامِ الصِبا
رَيِّقِ العُمرِ
passage.english:
Is there, for a lovesick man, from your scornful lips,
like the finest wine,
sips mixed with sugar
that grant delight —
sips handed down from the truest jewels,
from the souls’ desire,
from the crescent of beauty, from the gazelle of the dunes,
from the willow wand?
You have shut the gardens of union against me:
have pity, O Ridwan,
and pity me in this great torment,
that perhaps I may find rest.
And upon that face of light,
of radiant brightness,
from a grieving man, an amber-scented greeting spreads
for as long as morning breaks,
and the east wind’s hand bends the willows of the hills,
and the turtle-dove sings,
and my heart yearns for the days of youth,
the fresh bloom of life.

passage.original:
दुइ आँखिभौं त तयार छन्, तरवार पो किन चाहियो,
तिमी आफु मालिक भै गयौ, सरकार पो किन चाहियो ॥१॥
पहरा कडा छ कटाक्षको, हरदम् तयारि मुहारमा,
घर भन्नु भारि महल् न हो, दरवार पो किन चाहियो ॥२॥
कति चम्‌किलो छ हँसाइको, हिसिमा किरन् पनि दाँतको,
मणि मोति नीर जुहार् न हो, अरु हार पो किन चाहियो ॥३॥
passage.english:
Your two eyebrows stand ready as they are: why would you need a sword?
You have become the master yourself: why would you need a government? ॥1॥
The guard of your sidelong glance is strict, always ready in your face;
your home is a mighty palace already: why would you need a royal court? ॥2॥
How bright are the rays of your teeth when you laugh and smile!
Are they not jewels, pearls and gems? Why would you need any other necklace? ॥3॥

display.title: Meibloesems, III — Breek blanke meien van den Levensboom
display.english: May Blossoms, III — Break white May branches from the Tree of Life
display.creator: Hélène Swarth

passage.original:
Breek blanke meien van den Levensboom!
Nu is de Mei gekomen, ook voor mij.
Als witte vlinders fladdren ze ons voorbij,
De bloesemblaadren van mijn lentedroom.
Zie, dit is weelde: wandlen zij aan zij
In 't bloeiend Eden onzer liefde, loom
En stil van 't groot geluk, met teedren schroom
Ontvangen en gedragen, bang en blij.
Nu laat mij leunen aan uw borst, mijn lief,
En leg uw streelhand op mijn lokken zacht
En zeg of 't u wel heugt, die eerste brief,
Die eerste kus en o die winternacht,
Toen Liefde mij in 't hart sloop als een dief,
Nu scepter-zwaaiende in vorstinnepracht.
passage.english:
Break white May blossom from the Tree of Life!
Now May has come, for me as well.
Like white butterflies they flutter past us,
the blossom petals of my spring dream.
See, this is bliss: to wander side by side
in the blossoming Eden of our love, languid
and quiet with great happiness, with tender shyness
received and carried, fearful and glad.
Now let me lean against your breast, my love,
and lay your stroking hand softly on my hair,
and tell me if you remember it, that first letter,
that first kiss, and oh, that winter night
when Love crept into my heart like a thief,
and now waves his sceptre in the splendour of a queen.

title: Camomile Tea
creator: Katherine Mansfield
description: Domestic intimacy between lovers sharing tea.
provenance: Poems (Constable, London, 1923); poem dated 1916
translation: Original-language poem only. Modern translations and editorial material are separate. English passage: Original English text; not a translation. Lines 5–16; three consecutive stanzas. Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography.
rights: Public domain in USA - Project Gutenberg
contextNote: Katherine Mansfield left New Zealand for London at 19 and became one of the great short-story writers in English. She wrote this poem in 1916, months after her brother was killed in the First World War, and died of tuberculosis in 1923, aged 34.

passage.original:
How little I thought, a year ago,
In that horrible cottage upon the Lee
That he and I should be sitting so
And sipping a cup of camomile tea.
Light as feathers the witches fly,
The horn of the moon is plain to see;
By a firefly under a jonquil flower
A goblin toasts a bumble-bee.
We might be fifty, we might be five,
So snug, so compact, so wise are we!
Under the kitchen-table leg
My knee is pressing against his knee.

title: De invierno
creator: Rubén Darío
originalDate: 1890 (included in expanded Azul… edition; earlier publication not established)

passage.original:
En invernales horas, mirad a Carolina.
Medio apelotonada, descansa en el sillón,
envuelta con su abrigo de marta cibelina
y no lejos del fuego que brilla en el salón.
El fino angora blanco, junto a ella se reclina,
rozando con su hocico la falda de Alençón,
no lejos de las jarras de porcelana china
que medio oculta un biombo de seda del Japón.
Con sus sutiles filtros la invade un dulce sueño;
entro, sin hacer ruido; dejo mi abrigo gris;
voy a besar su rostro, rosado y halagüeño
como una rosa roja que fuera flor de lis;
abre los ojos; mírame, con su mirar risueño
y en tanto cae la nieve del cielo de París.
passage.english:
In the hours of winter, look at Carolina.
Half curled up, she rests in the armchair,
wrapped in her sable coat,
not far from the fire that glows in the drawing room.
The fine white angora lies beside her,
brushing her Alençon-lace skirt with its nose,
not far from the Chinese porcelain jars
half hidden by a Japanese silk screen.
With its subtle potions a sweet sleep steals over her;
I come in without a sound; I leave my grey coat;
I go to kiss her face, rosy and inviting
like a red rose that might be a fleur-de-lis;
she opens her eyes; she looks at me with her smiling gaze,
and meanwhile the snow falls from the Paris sky.

passage.original:
冬至ㅅᄃᆞᆯ 기나긴 밤을 한허리를 버혀 내여
春風 니불 아레 서리서리 너헛다가

passage.english:
I will cut the waist from the long, long night of the midwinter month,
and fold it, coil upon coil, under a quilt of spring breeze,
and on the night my love comes home, unroll it, fold by fold.

passage.original:
Бисеро моме, Бисеро,
што носиш бисер на грло?
Твоето грло хубаво
и от дробнаго бисера
хилјада пати побело.
Бисеро моме, Бисеро,
зошто со бисер покриваш
твоето грло хубаво?
Ја нејку бисер да баца,
тук сака твоето грло.
Бисеро моме, Бисеро,
за кого нижиш бисерот?
За кого готвиш дарои?
Ја дарој бисер не сака,
тук сака мома Бисера.
passage.english:
Bisera, my girl, Bisera,
why do you wear pearls at your throat?
Your lovely throat
is a thousand times whiter
than even the finest pearls.
Bisera, my girl, Bisera,
why do you cover with pearls
your lovely throat?
I don’t want to kiss pearls,
it is your throat I long for.
Bisera, my girl, Bisera,
for whom are you stringing the pearls?
For whom are you preparing gifts?
I want no gift of pearls,
I want the maiden Bisera.

passage.original:
De sidste gæster
vi fulgte til grinden;
farvellets rester
tog nattevinden.
I tifold øde
lå haven og huset,
hvor toner søde
mig nys berused.
Det var en fest kun,
før natten den sorte;
hun var en gæst kun, —
og nu er hun borte.
passage.english:
The last of the guests
we walked to the gate;
what was left of goodbye
the night wind took.
Ten times more empty
lay garden and house,
where sweet music
had made me drunk just now.
It was only a party
before the black night;
she was only a guest, —
and now she is gone.
