passage.original:
خليلي عوجا نمنحِ الربعَ ساعةً
تحيَّةَ جازٍ بالوفا غيرِ مُؤتلِ
ولسنا نحيَّي الدار حُبّاً لِربَعها
ولكنه حُبٌّ لكالأدم خُذَّلِ
شَناغيف هيفٍ ناعماتٍ نواهدٍ
أماليدَ غيدٍ من عرانين نهشَلِ
وفرْعاءَ غرَّاءِ المجرَّد طَفَلةٍ
من الخفرات الغُنِّ شمّا المقَّبلِ
لها مقلتا مَذعورةٍ أم جوذرٍ
وسالفتا براقَةِ الجيد مُغزِلِ
وتستر مَتْنَيها بأسحمَ فاحمٍ
كثيفٍ أثيثِ النّبت جعد المرجّلِ
وتَبسمُ عن غُرٍّ كأن وميضها
تلألؤُ برقٍ في حبيٍّ مكلَّلِ
passage.english:
My two friends, turn aside; let us give this camp an hour,
the greeting of one who repays in full and never falls short.
We do not greet the dwelling out of love for its ground,
but for love of women like white gazelles that linger behind the herd,
tall and slender, soft and young,
supple and graceful, from the noblest of Nahshal;
and for one with long hair, gleaming where her skin is bare, tender,
one of the modest, soft-voiced girls, her mouth sweet to kiss;
she has the eyes of a startled doe with her fawn,
and the neck of a gazelle with a gleaming throat;
she hides her back beneath hair black as charcoal,
thick and abundant, curling where it is combed;
and she smiles, showing white teeth whose gleam
is like lightning flashing in a heaped-up cloud.

passage.original:
رانجھا رانجھا کردی نی میں آپے رانجھا ہوئی
سدّو نی مینُوں دھیدو رانجھا، ہِیر نہ آکھو کوئی
رانجھا میں وِچ، میں رانجھے وِچ، مینوں ہور خیال نہ کوئی
میں نہیں اوہ آپ ہے اپنی، آپ کرے دلجوئی
جو کوئی ساڈے اندر وسّے، ذات اساڈی سو ای
ہَتّھ کُھونڈی میرے اگے مَنگُو، موڈھے بُھورا لوئی
بُلّھا ہیر سَلیٹی ویکھو، کِتّھے جا کھلوئی
جس دے نال میں نیونہہ لگایا، اوہو جیہی ہوئی
تخت ہزارے لے چل بُلھیا، سیالِیں ملے نہ ڈھوئی
passage.english:
Calling “Ranjha, Ranjha”, O friends, I myself have become Ranjha.
Call me Dhido Ranjha, friends; let no one call me Heer.
Ranjha is in me, I am in Ranjha; I have no other thought.
It is not I: it is he himself, who comforts his own heart.
The one who dwells within us is our very being.
A herder’s staff in my hand, the herd before me, a brown blanket on my shoulders.
Bulleh, look at Heer of the Sial clan: where has she come to stand!
The one I have given my love to, I have become just like him.
Take me to Takht Hazara, Bulleh; among the Sials I find no shelter.

passage.original:
Ṭalʿat nigmet il-ġarrār min rād,
u-marbāha gabal Ḥaurān min rād;
billa yā hawa l-ġaddār indār min rād,
nada wa-kṭur ʿala ṣidr il-ḥabāba.
Nizil maʿ bēn Yāfa u-bēn Maʿlūl,
tiḥkīni u-band it-tōb maḥlūl;
ana-lli min frāḳ il-ḥubb maʿlūl,
u-mā yišfīni ġēr šōf il-iḥbāba.
Nizil maʿ bēn Ṣāfīta u-ʿAkkār,
u-kāsi kān ṣāfīli tʿakkar;
ḥabābi lau saḳūni samm sukkar,
ʿala ḳalbi aladd min eš-šarāba.
Nizil maʿ bēn Zaḥle w-il-Ksaijir,
ḥabībi lā ṭawīl walā ksaijir;
ḥalafna dīn ʿannak mā nġaijir,
mā zāl er-rūḥ wi-ggitti ṣawāba.

passage.original:
Yo quisiera decírtelo y no puedo;
me lo veda un poder que no es humano.
Te voy a hablar y una invisible mano
posa en mis labios trémulos un dedo.
Mudo, y absorto, y aturdido quedo
ante el prodigio de este amor arcano,
tan azul, tan sin fin como un océano,
tan hondo que a mí mismo me da miedo.
Miedo, pavor de que también me ames;
de que así como yo toda te inflames
en este amor cuyo final no vemos;
porque he asomado a mi alma entre mí mismo
y no hallo el fondo del profundo abismo
de amor y de dolor en que caeremos.
passage.english:
I would like to tell you, and I cannot;
a power that is not human forbids me.
I am about to speak, and an invisible hand
lays a finger on my trembling lips.
Mute, absorbed and dazed I stand
before the wonder of this secret love,
as blue, as endless as an ocean,
so deep that I myself am afraid.
Afraid, in dread that you love me too;
that, like me, you may be all aflame
in this love whose end we cannot see;
for I have looked into my soul, within myself,
and cannot find the bottom of the deep abyss
of love and pain into which we shall fall.

passage.original:
Chopĩ haitýpe mokói oĩva,
ndojohejávai maramoĩte;
peteĩchaitéva hữngue porãme
ha iporãnguépe katu kõingue.
Upe hữnguépe he’i jakúpe
ha pyharépe: tapomohữ.
Tesapehápe he’i jasýpe
ku oike potávo: toroipyru.
Ma’ẽ saguýpe jahechapáma
Ka’a pa’ữme kuarahysẽ
ha om’ẽmbápe nahesakãiri
hendy porãnte jasyichaite.
Mba’e mbyasýpe "luto" voíva
ha vy’ahápe tory rupa
Ma’ẽ hatãme chemopirĩva
ma’ẽ mbeguépe chemoãngaipa.
Omoporãva kuñataĩnguéra
jáma hi’áva, jáma hete,
pe pende jara noikotevẽiri
porã oñohẽgui pende pire.
passage.english:
Two chopí birds that share one nest
never leave each other at all;
exactly alike in their lovely blackness,
and in their beauty, twins indeed.
With that blackness they tell the jacu bird
and the night: “Let me make you darker.”
With their brightness they tell the moon,
as it is about to set: “Let me step over you.”
In a sidelong glance we see already
the sunrise between the woods;
and when they look full on, they are not only bright:
they blaze with beauty, just like the moon.
In sorrow, mourning ready-made;
in gladness, a bed of joy;
with a hard look they make me shiver,
with a gentle look they lead me into sin.
What makes young women lovely,
be it their hair, be it their body,
the one who owns you has no need of:
beauty spills from your very skin.

passage.original:
Qué estará haciendo esta hora mi andina y dulce Rita
de junco y capulí;
ahora que me asfixia Bizancio, y que dormita
la sangre, como flojo cognac, dentro de mí.
Dónde estarán sus manos que en actitud contrita
planchaban en las tardes blancuras por venir;
ahora, en esta lluvia que me quita
las ganas de vivir.
Qué será de su falda de franela; de sus
afanes; de su andar;
de su sabor a cañas de mayo del lugar.
Ha de estarse a la puerta mirando algún celaje,
y al fin dirá temblando: «Qué frío hay... Jesús!»
y llorará en las tejas un pájaro salvaje.
passage.english:
What can my sweet Andean Rita be doing at this hour,
Rita of reeds and wild cherries,
now that Byzantium stifles me, and my blood
drowses inside me like weak cognac?
Where can her hands be, which, as if in penitence,
ironed in the evenings whitenesses still to come,
now, in this rain that takes from me
the wish to live?
What has become of her flannel skirt, of her
toil, of her walk,
of her taste of the local May sugar cane?
She must be standing at the door, watching the sunset clouds,
and at last she will say, shivering: “How cold it is… Jesus!”
and on the roof tiles a wild bird will weep.

passage.original:
Cong pag saulang cong basahin sa isip
ang nañgacaraang arao ñg pag-ibig,
may mahahaguilap cayang natititic
liban na cay Celiang namugad sa dibdib?
Yaong Celiang laguing pinañgañganiban
baca macalimot sa pag-iibigan;
ang iquinalubog niyaring capalaran
sa lubhang malalim na caralitaan.
Macaligtaang co cayang di basahin
nagdaáng panahón ñg suyuan namin?
caniyang pagsintáng guinugol sa aquin
at pinuhunan cong pagod at hilahil?
Lumipas ang arao na lubhang matamis
at ualáng nátira condi ang pag-ibig ,
tapat na pag suyong lalagui sa dibdib
hanggang sa libiñgan bangcay co,i, maidlip.
passage.english:
When I go back and read over in my mind
the days of love that have passed,
can anything be found written there
except Celia, who nested in my heart?
That Celia whom I always feared
might forget our love;
the one who sank this fortune of mine
into the deepest poverty.
Could I neglect to read over
the past time of our courtship,
the love she spent on me,
and the toil and sorrow I gave for it?
The sweetest days have gone by,
and nothing is left but love,
a faithful devotion that will stay in my heart
until my body sleeps in the grave.

passage.original:
Ledwiem ciebie zobaczył, jużem się zapłonił,
W nieznaném oku dawnéj znajomości pytał,
I s twych jagód wzajemny rumieniec wykwitał
Jak z róży, któréj piersi zaranek odsłonił.
Ledwieś piosnkę zaczęła, jużem łzy uronił,
Twój głos wnikał do serca i za duszę chwytał;
Zdało się że ją anioł po imieniu witał,
I w zegar niebios chwilę zbawienia zadzwonił.
O luba! niech twe oczy przyznać się nie boją,
Jeśli cię mém spojrzeniem, jeśli głosem wzruszę,
Nie dbam że los i ludzie przeciwko nam stoją,
Że uciekać i kochać bez nadziei muszę.
Niech ślub ziemski innego darzy ręką twoją,
Tylko wyznaj że Bóg mi poślubił twą duszę.
passage.english:
I had barely seen you when I blushed,
and sought an old acquaintance in an unknown eye,
and an answering blush bloomed on your cheeks
as from a rose whose breast the dawn has bared.
You had barely begun your song when I shed tears;
your voice entered my heart and seized my soul;
it seemed an angel greeted it by name
and struck the hour of salvation on heaven’s clock.
O beloved! let your eyes not be afraid to confess
if my glance, if my voice, moves you;
I do not care that fate and people stand against us,
that I must flee, and love without hope.
Let an earthly marriage give your hand to another;
only confess that God has wedded your soul to mine.

passage.original:
Pe genunchii mei ședea-vei,
Vom fi singuri-singurei,
Iar în păr, înfiorate,
Or să-ți cadă flori de tei.
Fruntea albă-n părul galben
Pe-al meu braț încet s-o culci,
Lăsând pradă gurii mele
Ale tale buze dulci...
Vom visa un vis ferice,
Îngâna-ne-vor c-un cânt
Singuratice izvoare,
Blânda batere de vânt;
passage.english:
You will sit upon my knees,
we'll be alone, all on our own,
and in your hair, all trembling,
the lime-tree flowers will fall.
Your white brow in your golden hair
you'll lay down gently on my arm,
leaving to my mouth as plunder
those sweet lips of yours…
We'll dream a happy dream,
and lulling us with their song
will be the lonely springs,
the gentle beating of the wind;

passage.original:
Meus olhos são como a noite
em que astro nenhum flutua
mas se o teu olhar o fita
na noite desponta a lua
Meu olhar é retratista
ò minha doce miragem
senão diz-me porque tenho
no meu peito a tua imagem
Roubei-te o primeiro beijo
o segundo foi-me dado
o terceiro, francamente,
creio que me foi roubado
Um dia a espuma dos mares
ao ver em si meu amor
Foi dizer baixinho à praia
– a Vénus mudou de cor
A nossa terra é tão bela
duma beleza sem par
E por ser assim formosa
Fê-la sua amante o mar…
passage.english:
My eyes are like the night
in which no star is floating,
but if your gaze rests on them,
the moon rises in that night.
My gaze is a portrait painter,
O my sweet mirage;
otherwise tell me why I carry
your image in my breast.
I stole the first kiss from you,
the second was given to me,
the third, frankly,
I believe was stolen from me.
One day the foam of the seas,
seeing my love reflected in it,
went and whispered to the shore:
'Venus has changed her colour.'
Our land is so lovely,
of a beauty without equal,
and because it is so fair
the sea has made it his lover…

passage.original:
А наша деца песме су моје,
тих састанака вечити траг;
то се не пише, то се не поје,
само што душом пробије зрак.
То разумемо само нас двоје,
то је у рају приновак драг,
то тек у заносу пророци слуте,
Santa Maria della Salute.
А кад ми дође да прсне глава
о тог живота хридовит крај,
најлепши сан ми постаће јава,
мој ропац њено: „Ево ме, нај!”
Из ништавила у славу слава,
из безњенице у рај, у рај!
У рај, у рај, у њезин загрљај!
Све ће се жеље ту да пробуде,
душине жице све да прогуде,
задивићемо светске колуте,
богове силне, камо ли људе,
звездама ћемо померит’ путе,
сунцима засут’ сељенске студе,
да у све куте зоре заруде,
да од милине дуси полуде,
Santa Maria della Salute.
passage.english:
And our children are my poems,
the everlasting trace of those meetings;
it cannot be written, it cannot be sung,
only a ray breaks through the soul.
Only the two of us understand it;
in paradise it is a dear new arrival;
only prophets in rapture can sense it,
Santa Maria della Salute.
And when my head comes to shatter
against the rocky shore of this life,
my loveliest dream will come true,
and my death rattle will be her “Here I am, my dearest!”
From nothingness into the glory of glories,
from a life without her into paradise, paradise!
Into paradise, paradise, into her embrace!
There every desire will awaken,
all the strings of the soul will ring out,
we will astonish the circling worlds,
the mighty gods, let alone mortals,
we will shift the paths of the stars,
shower the cold of the universe with suns,
so that dawns blush in every corner,
so that spirits go mad with delight,
Santa Maria della Salute.

Tanjong Katong ayer-nya biru,
Tempat berlaboh kochi Malaka;
Sedang sa-kampong lagi ku-rindu,
Inikan pula jauh di-mata.
Kalau tidak karna kunchi,
Papan peti sahaya belahkan;
Kalau tidak karna mati,
Belah dada sahaya tunjokkan.
Anak berok besar lengan,
Masok ka-bendang makan padi;
Kalau kaseh alang-alangan,
Biar ta’usah sa-kali-kali.

Hilang di-bungkus puncha kain;

passage.original:
Či vieš ešte, ako sme raz
v jasný večer spolu stáli
a ku hviezdam trblietavým
v dumách tichých pozerali?
Jak sme striehli obidvaja,
až by spadla hviezda dolu,
bo sme oba, poverčive,
niečo žiadať mali vôľu.
Dobrobyt ty nášho ľudu
chcel si si vraj žiadať skryte
a ja — ach, mnou zachvievali
túžby divné, neurčité…
„Blaho to vraj v hviezdach žiari,“
dumala som, rozochvelá;
„keby, ach, tá hviezdka jasná
dolu ku mne zletieť chcela!“
Tu sme oba k nebu zreli
naladení milým klamom:
sťaby hviezdka padajúca
mala nám byť talizmanom.
V tom sa stretli zraky naše
divnou mocou upútané —;
a za ten čas tichým letom
padla hviezda z nebies báne.
Kým sa stretli zraky naše,
zhasol hviezdy plápol skvelý,
vysloviť však svoje túžby
oba sme my zapomneli.
Však mne predsa splnila sa
blúznivá tá túžba kási,
odvtedy to v srdci mojom
sťaby plno hviezdnej krásy.
passage.english:
Do you still remember how once
we stood together on a clear evening
and gazed up at the twinkling stars,
lost in quiet thoughts?
How we both kept watch
for a star to fall,
because we both, superstitious,
had a mind to wish for something.
You meant, so you said, to wish in secret
for the well-being of our people,
and I — ah, I was trembling with
strange, uncertain longings…
“They say bliss shines in the stars,”
I mused, all a-tremble;
“if only, ah, that bright little star
would fly down to me!”
Then we both looked up to the sky,
tuned to a sweet illusion,
as if a falling star
were meant to be our talisman.
At that moment our eyes met,
held by a strange power;
and in that time, in silent flight,
a star fell from heaven’s dome.
While our eyes were meeting,
the star’s splendid flame went out,
but to speak our wishes
we both forgot.
And yet for me it came true,
that dreamy longing of mine;
since then, in my heart,
it is as if all were full of starry beauty.

passage.original:
Šáqlan Gédi-bā šára-ʾál-áy
lō šir tágayá-yay,
wáḥan ḥámar šakamádda
ū gū ḥiḍay,
šámis rúgtōdi-yay.
šeḥyáda ʿílmiga šéga-yáy
šáraf wádagán-i.
Gāšánka ī šaqal,
míd-dan šegayá tímid-i.
Marākíbta badáha márta
ē málabka díqaysa;
wáḥa ī ga gá muq ḍēr Ijo
an méher kū tūbáyay.
passage.english:
Shaqlan, daughter of Gedi, truly:
crowds go out to her;
I too put the reins
on a bay horse
and rode towards the house of the sun.
The sheikhs who teach learning
have a share in her refinement.
Cover my shield for me:
the one I speak of has come.
The ships sail the seas
and bring precious things;
but I would rather gaze at Ijo,
for whom I paid the bride-price.

passage.original:
Zwei Segel erhellend
Die tiefblaue Bucht!
Zwei Segel sich schwellend
Zu ruhiger Flucht!
Wie eins in den Winden
Sich wölbt und bewegt,
Wird auch das Empfinden
Des andern erregt.
Begehrt eins zu hasten,
Das andre geht schnell,
Verlangt eins zu rasten,
Ruht auch sein Gesell.
passage.english:
Two sails lighting up
the deep blue bay!
Two sails filling
for a peaceful run!
As one, in the winds,
bellies and stirs,
so the feeling
of the other is moved.
If one wants to hurry,
the other goes fast;
if one longs to rest,
its partner rests too.

passage.original:
أرَاكَ عَصِيَّ الدَّمْعِ شِيمَتُكَ الصَّبْرُ
أمَا لِلْهَوَى نَهْيٌ عَلَيْكَ وَلا أمْر
بَلَى أنَا مُشْتَاقٌ وَعِنْدِي لَوْعَةٌ
وَلَكِنَّ مِثْلِي لا يُذَاعُ لَهُ سِرُّ
إذَا اللَّيْلُ أضْوَانِي بَسَطتُ يَدَ الهَوَى
وَأذْلَلْتُ دَمْعًا مِنْ خَلائِقِهِ الْكِبْرُ
تَكَادُ تُضِيءُ النَّارُ بَيْنَ جَوَانِحِي
إذَا هِيَ أذْكَتْهَا الصَّبَابَةُ وَالْفِكْرُ
مُعَلِّلَتِي بالْوَصْلِ وَالموت دُونَهُ
إذَا مِتُّ ظَمْآنًا فَلا نَزَلَ الْقَطْرُ
حَفِظْتُ وَضَيَّعْتِ الموَدَّةَ بَيْنَنَا
وَأحْسَنُ مِنْ بَعْضِ الْوَفَاءِ لَكِ الْعُذْرُ
وَمَا هَذِهِ الأيَّامُ إلا صَحَائِفُ
لأحْرُفِهَا مِنْ كَفِّ كَاتِبِهَا بِشْرُ
بِنَفْسِي مِنَ الْغَادِينَ في الحيِّ غَادَةٌ
هَوَايَ لَهَا ذَنْبٌ وَبَهْجَتُهَا عُذْرُ
passage.english:
I see you dry-eyed; patience is your nature:
has love no command or forbidding over you?
Yes, I am full of longing, and I burn,
but a man like me does not let his secret be told.
When night enfolds me, I stretch out the hand of love
and humble tears whose nature is pride.
The fire between my ribs almost blazes into light
when longing and brooding fan it.
You put me off with promises of union, but death stands before it:
if I die of thirst, may no rain ever fall.
I kept faith, and you squandered the love between us;
but making excuses for you suits me better than some kinds of loyalty.
These days are nothing but pages
whose letters glow with the hand of the one who writes them.
My life for one young woman among those leaving the camp at dawn:
my love for her is a sin, and her beauty its excuse.

passage.original:
She hastily and eagerly glanced over it, raised her head for a time, and then read, and read, and read again.
The letter was this:—
“Lady, though I am a pirate, recoil not from me.
I am sensible to the feelings of honor, and need not be feared by any lady;
in the uprightness of my soul I have dared to love you;
deign to cast but one look on me, and let me believe I may hope.
Lorenzo.”
Agnes read this over and over again in nervous trepidation, then folded it, and put it by.
She was a victim to strong contending emotions.
She felt she knew not what for Lorenzo, but he was a pirate.

عذبةٌ أنتِ كالطفولةِ ، كالأحلامِ ،
كاللحنِ ، كالصباحِ الجديدِ
كالسماءِ الضحوكِ كالليلةِ القَمْراءِ ،
كالوردِ ، كابتسامِ الوليدِ
يا لها من وداعةٍ وجَمالِ
وشبابٍ مُنَعَّمٍ أُمْلُودِ !
يا لها من طهارةٍ ، تَبْعَثُ التقْديـ
ـسَ في مهجةِ الشَّقِيِّ العَنِيدِ ! . . .
يا لها رقَّةً تكادُ يَرُفُّ الوَرْ
دُ منها في الصخرةِ الجلمودِ !
أَيُّ شيءٍ أنتِ ؟! هل أنتِ «فينسُ»
تهادتْ بين الورَى من جديدِ
لِتُعِيدَ الشبابَ والفرحَ للمَغْـ
ـمُومِ لِلعالَمِ التعيسِ العَمِيدِ !
أم مَلاكُ الفردوسِ جاء إلى الأرْ
ضِ لِيُحْيِيَ روحَ السلامِ العَهِيدِ !
أنتِ . . . ، ما أنتِ ؟ رسمٌ جميلٌ
عبقريٌّ من فنِّ هذا الوجودِ
فيكِ ما فيه من غموضٍ وعُمْقٍ
وجمالٍ مُقَدَّسٍ معبودِ
passage.english:
You are sweet as childhood, as dreams,
as a melody, as a new morning,
as the laughing sky, as the moonlit night,
as the rose, as a newborn’s smile.
What gentleness, what beauty,
what soft and supple youth!
What purity, that wakes reverence
even in the heart of the wretched and stubborn!
What tenderness: roses could almost flutter
from it even in solid rock!
What are you? Are you Venus,
walking once more among humankind
to bring back youth and joy to the grieving,
to the miserable, heartsick world?
Or an angel of paradise come down to earth
to revive the spirit of a peace long gone?
You… what are you? A lovely picture,
a masterpiece of the art of this existence;
in you is all its mystery and depth
and its holy, worshipped beauty.

passage.original:
Хотіла б я тебе, мов плющ, обняти,
Так міцно, щільно, і закрить од світа,
Я не боюсь тобі життя одняти,
Ти будеш мов руїна, листом вкрита, —
Плющ їй дає життя, він обіймає,
Боронить від негоди стіну голу,
Але й руїна стало так тримає
Товариша, аби не впав додолу.
Їм добре так удвох, — як нам з тобою, —
А прийде час розсипатись руїні, —
Нехай вона плюща сховає під собою.
Навіщо здався плющ у самотині?
passage.english:
I would like to wrap my arms around you like ivy,
so tight, so close, and shut you off from the world;
I'm not afraid I'd take your life away,
you'd be like a ruin covered in leaves, —
ivy gives it life, it holds it close,
it shields the bare wall from bad weather,
but the ruin, too, holds on so steadily
to its companion, so that it won't fall.
They're happy together, like you and me, —
and when the time comes for the ruin to crumble,
let it hide the ivy underneath itself.
What good would ivy be on its own?

title: Sonnet 18
creator: William Shakespeare
editionDate: Print edition not identified; digital release 1997
description: The beloved is preserved in verse.
provenance: Sonnets; first published 1609
translation: Original-language poem only. Modern translations and editorial material are separate. English passage: Original English text; not a translation. Complete sonnet, 14 lines; spelling follows linked edition. Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography.

contextNote: Shakespeare's sonnets were published in 1609, though many were probably written in the 1590s. Most of the first 126, including this one, are addressed to a young man; its promise that verse will outlast its subject has held for four centuries.

passage.original:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature's changing course untrimm'd:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow'st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander'st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow'st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
passage.english:

Nor shall death brag thou wander'st in his shade,

So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

title: Wild nights! Wild nights!
creator: Emily Dickinson
editionDate: 1891 (Todd/Higginson edition)
description: Erotic longing through sea and harbour imagery.
provenance: Poems, Series Two (1891); editors T. W. Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd
translation: Use this early edited text. Modern Johnson/Franklin editions differ and have separate copyright considerations. English passage: Original English text; not a translation. Complete poem, 12 lines; punctuation follows 1891 editorial version reproduced by Gutenberg. Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography.
rights: Public domain in USA - Project Gutenberg
contextNote: Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems in Amherst, Massachusetts, but only about ten were published in her lifetime. Her first editors hesitated over printing this one in 1891 because of its passion; whom it was written for is still debated.

passage.original:
Wild nights! Wild nights!
Were I with thee,
Wild nights should be
Our luxury!
Futile the winds
To a heart in port, —
Done with the compass,
Done with the chart.
Rowing in Eden!
Ah! the sea!
Might I but moor
To-night in thee!
passage.english:
Wild nights! Wild nights!
Were I with thee,
Wild nights should be
Our luxury!
Futile the winds
To a heart in port, —
Done with the compass,
Done with the chart.
Rowing in Eden!
Ah! the sea!
Might I but moor
To-night in thee!

title: Explosión
creator: Delmira Agustini
editionDate: Undated transcription of the 1907 poem
description: Affirmative: love dispels melancholy and fills life with energy, kisses and laughter.
provenance: El libro blanco (Frágil), 1907; Instituto Cervantes confirms the collection/date
translation: Original-language poem only; modern translations and recordings are separate. Retain attribution and source/license links for copyrightable transcription material. English passage: Earlier English draft by ChatGPT (replaced); draft for editorial review. Complete sonnet, 14 lines. Original and English cells contain the same selection; line breaks are reading lines, not a claim of manuscript typography. Translation redone (30 October 2026) for the anthology review: fresh English translation by Claude (Anthropic AI) made directly from the original text, without reference to any other translation; draft for editorial review.
rights: Public-domain original; site transcription has CC BY-SA terms where applicable
contextNote: Delmira Agustini published this poem at 20 and became one of the first women in Latin America to write openly about desire. In 1914 she was killed by her former husband, weeks after a divorce made possible by Uruguay's new divorce law.

passage.original:
¡Si la vida es amor, bendita sea!
¡Quiero más vida para amar! Hoy siento
que no valen mil años de la idea
lo que un minuto azul del sentimiento.
Mi corazón moría triste y lento...
Hoy abre en luz como una flor febea;
¡la vida brota como un mar violento
donde la mano del amor golpea!
Hoy, partió hacia la noche, triste, fría,
rotas las alas mi melancolía;
como una vieja mancha del dolor
en la sombra lejana se deslíe...
¡Mi vida toda canta, besa, ríe!
¡Mi vida toda es una boca en flor!
passage.english:
If life is love, then blessed be it!
I want more life so I can love! Today I feel
that a thousand years of thinking are not worth
one blue minute of feeling.
My heart was dying, sad and slow…
Today it opens in light like a flower of Phoebus;
life wells up like a violent sea
where love's hand strikes!
Today, sad and cold, my melancholy
left for the night with broken wings;
like an old stain of grief
it fades away in the distant shadow…
My whole life sings, kisses, laughs!
My whole life is a mouth in flower!

title: Muhabbatsiz kishi odam emasdur
titleEnglish: A person without love is not truly human (first line)
creator: Nodira (Mohlaroyim)
originalDate: Early 19th century; before author’s death in 1842
editionDate: Undated modern Uzbek-script transcription

display.title: Muhabbatsiz kishi odam emasdur
display.english: A person without love is not truly human
display.creator: Nodira

passage.original:
Na gul sayr ayla, na fikri bahor et,
Jahondin kech, xayoli vasli yor et.
Muhabbatsiz kishi odam emasdur,
Gar odamsan, muhabbat ixtiyor et.
Uzoru qaddu raftoringni koʻrsat,
Chaman sarvu gulini sharmisor et.
Labi maxmurdadurmen, jomi may tut,
Karam qil, soqiyo, daf’i humor et.
«Analhaq» mojarosin aylading fosh,
kel, ey Mansur, istiqboli dor et.
Duru ashku aqiqi xuni dilni
Kelu yoring ayogʻigʻa nisor et.
Kuyib, ey Nodira, olam eligʻa
Muhabbat shevasini oshkor et.
passage.english:
Do not stroll among the roses, do not think of spring:
give up the world, and dream of union with your beloved.
A person without love is not truly human:
if you are human, choose love.
Show your cheek, your stature and your walk,
and put the garden’s cypress and rose to shame.
My lips are parched with longing; hand me the cup of wine;
be generous, cupbearer, and ease my aching head.
You made public the secret of “I am the Truth”:
come, O Mansur, go out to meet the gallows.
The pearls of your tears, the carnelian of your heart’s blood:
come, and scatter them at your beloved’s feet.
Burning, O Nodira, before the people of the world,
reveal the ways of love.

passage.original:
Solitaria, sin ventura,
Fija en la onda la mirada,
Llena el alma de amargura,
Desgarrado el corazón,
Virgen triste, abandonada
Pide á Dios consolación.
Aun divisa en lontananza
Del bajel la blanca estela ;
Imagina su esperanza
Que á su amante abraza ya;
Si columbra alguna vela,
Hondo grito al aire da.
Hace un año que la hermosa,
Que suspira sin consuelo,
Angustiada, temblorosa,
Á su amante vio partir;
Y enlutado vio del cielo
El purísimo zafir.
passage.english:
Alone, without fortune,
her gaze fixed on the waves,
her soul full of bitterness,
her heart torn apart,
a sad, abandoned maiden
begs God for consolation.
In the distance she can still make out
the white wake of the ship;
in her hope she imagines
that she already holds her lover;
if she glimpses a sail,
she sends a deep cry into the air.
It is a year since the lovely one,
who sighs without comfort,
anguished and trembling,
watched her lover depart,
and saw the purest sapphire
of the sky dressed in mourning.

display.title: Miếng trầu / Mời trầu
display.english: A Piece of Betel / Offering Betel
display.creator: Hồ Xuân Hương

passage.original:
Quả cau nho nhỏ, miếng giầu hôi,
Này của Xuân-Hương mới quệt rồi.
Có phải duyên nhau, thì thắm lại,
Đừng xanh như lá, bạc như vôi.
passage.english:
A tiny areca nut, a humble betel quid:
here, Xuân Hương has just spread the lime on it.
If we are fated for each other, let it turn deep red;
do not stay green as the leaf, or turn pale and faithless as the lime.

display.title: طرب الفؤاد لطيف روضة غاشي
display.english: My heart thrilled at Rawda's phantom
display.creator: Waddah al-Yaman

passage.original:
طربَ الفؤاد لطيفِ روضةَ غاشي
والقومُ بين أباطحٍ وعشاشِ
أنَّى اهتديتِ ودونَ أرضكِ سبسبٌ
قَفْرٌ وحَزْنٌ في دُجىً ورِشاشِ
قالتْ: تكاليفُ المحبِّ كلفتها
إنَّ المحِبَّ إذا أُخيفَ لَماشِي
أدعوكِ روضةَ رحبٍ واسمكِ غيرهُ
شفقاً وأخشى أن يشي بكِ واشي
قَالَتْ: فَزُرْنا قلتُ كيفَ أزُورُكم
وأنا امرُؤٌ لِخُروجِ سِرِّكِ خاشِي
قَالَتْ: فكُنْ لِعُمومَتي سَلْماً مَعاً
والطفْ لإخوتيَ الذين تماشي
فَتَزورَنا معهُم زيارةَ آمنٍ
والسرُّ يا وَضَّاحُ لَيس بفَاشِي
ولقيتها تمشي بأبطحَ مرةً
بِخلاخِلٍ وبِحُلَّةٍ أكْباشِ
فَظَلِلْتُ مَعْمُوداً وبِتُّ مُسَهَّداً
ودموعُ عيني في الرداءِ غواشي
يا رَوْضُ حُبُّكِ سَلَّ جِسمي وانْتَحى
فِي العَظْمِ حتى قدْ بَلَغْتِ مُشاشِي
passage.english:
My heart thrilled when Rawda's phantom came to me
while the company slept among the valleys and the scrub.
How did you find your way, when between us and your land
lies a waste, empty and rugged, in darkness and drizzle?
She said: I have taken on the burdens of one who loves;
a lover, even when threatened, keeps on walking.
I call you “Rawda of the open plain”, though your name is another,
out of care, for I fear some tale-bearer will betray you.
She said: Then come and visit us. I said: How can I visit you,
when I am a man who dreads your secret coming out?
She said: Then make your peace with all my uncles,
and be kind to my brothers when you walk with them;
then you can visit us with them, as one who is safe,
and the secret, Waddah, will not get out.
And once I met her walking in a valley,
in anklets and a fine striped robe;
all day I was lovesick, all night I lay awake,
and the tears of my eyes soaked my cloak.
O Rawd, your love has wasted my body and pressed on
into the bone, until it has reached the marrow.
